items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER

that a parliamentarian from the Riksdag of Sweden, Dr Anders W Jonsson MP, is
present in the gallery. I am sure that members would wish that he be welcomed.
Skycity, Convention Centre—Advice to Cabinet
1. METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Minister for Economic

items.speaker: Development
items.text: When he said, in relation to the Skycity convention centre deal, “the
negotiated significant additional harm-minimisation measures that apply to all gambling
machines in that casino will together act to reduce harm” was he basing his claim on the
Health Ministry’s gambling harm minimisation team’s advice; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: My comment was
based on information contained in the regu latory impact statem ent prepared by the
Ministry of Business, Innovation and Empl oyment following consultation with, and
summarising advice received from, the followi ng agencies: the Ministry of Justice, the
Gambling Commission, the Ministry of Pacific Island Affairs, Te Puni Kōkiri, Treasury,
the Ministry of Social Devel opment, the Ministry of Women’s Affairs, the Office of
Ethnic Affairs, the Department of Internal  Affairs, the New Zealand Police, and the
Ministry of Health.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Why did the Minister exclude from the regulatory impact statement
the advice from the Ministry of Health that it was “doubtful” voluntary pre-commit
cards would reduce harm, and that Skycity wa s already using the t echnology so it was
not, in fact, either new or additional?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I think the member misunde rstands the role of the
regulatory impact statement. The regulatory imp act statement is prepared by officials,
and it is a summary of all the different o fficial advice that comes from different
agencies.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Why, then, did the Minister sign off on the regulatory impact
statement, which excluded the advice from the Ministry of Health  that doubling of host
responsibility staff at the Skycity Casino was likely to have at best a minimal effect?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Again I think the member is misunderstanding the role of
the regulatory impact statement, which is to collect together the information supplied by
different departments. It may come as a surpri se to the member that I have not read the
advice from every single one of those agencies. The regulatory impact statement—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Why not? You’re in charge.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Do not be a clown, Trevor. The regulatory impact
statement is put together as a summary of the different agencies.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Is it not his practice to read the advice from all officials on
bills?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: It is not my practice to read advice to individual Ministers
from every single agency for a paper that I am taking to Cabinet. I very much doubt that
13230 Questions for Oral Answer 4 Sep 2013
it is any Minister’s practice, and it was certa inly not the practice of previous Ministers
in the previous Government.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: When the Minister told this House that Cabinet had considered “all
of the risks and benefits of the social a nd economic impacts” of this deal, was he
mistaken, or was he deliberately misleading the House?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, neither. Cabinet, as always in these situations,
receives a Cabinet paper, and in appropria te cases, including this one, a regulatory
impact assessment, which different agencies contribute to and which is summarised by
the lead agency, is then taken to Cabinet. That is what occurred in this case, as occurs in
a whole range of other cases. It has to be said that the regulatory impact statements have
been a heck of a lot better prepared unde r this Government than under previous
Governments.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: What other advice did the Minister choose to leave out of the
regulatory impact statement, and did part of it include  the advice on the intended
reduction in the Television New Zealand (TVNZ) dividend as a result of the sale of land
to Skycity under the convention centre deal?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Again, for the member’s benefit, if she had listened to a
previous answer, she would notice that the suppo sition contained in the first part of that
supplementary question is incorrect. In rela tion to the second part of the supplementary
question, she is also incorrect because, in ac tual fact, in terms of the forgiveness of
dividends, which was flagged, potentially, some time ago, that is for the opportunity for
TVNZ to renovate its building next door, whic h I think is a fantastic outcome. It has
sold some land to Skycity as part of the convention centre arrangements and it is getting
an opportunity to make a much-needed renovation to its facilities.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Were Cabinet and his caucus colleagues made aware of the likely
significant extra cost of this need to induce TVNZ by way of a reduced dividend
expectation to move out of part of its cen tral Auckland premises to make way for the
convention centre deal before they voted for the bill?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I completely reject the asse rtion that the member makes.
The reality, as I have made quite clear, is that the convention centre could proceed with
this extra piece of land or without, and it is quite obvious that it could do so. TVNZ was
given the opportunity to sell the land. It we nt to its shareholding Ministers and said:
“Well, look, we would like to renovate our building. Would you support us in doing
so?”. As has been said publicly for some time now, it was indicated that shareholding
Ministers would support that, and so out of this we will get a fantastic convention centre
for New Zealand based in the middle of Auckland City, generating jobs, generating
tourism opportunities, and also TVNZ, next door, will get an upgrade of its building,
including earthquake strengthening and future -proofing. So it is all working out as a
pretty big win-win.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Did the Minister advise the Minister of Broadcasting, Craig Foss, last
year about the possibility of a reduced divi dend from TVNZ due to the Skycity deal,
given that Mr Foss demanded at least 9 percent in dividends from TVNZ in December?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I think the matter was raised by TVNZ with its
shareholding Ministers a reas onably short time ago. There wa s a letter that went back,
which I referred to publicly, I think, from memory, a coupl e of months ago, and it was
probably shortly before that. So I think that relating it to last year is probably reasonably
irrelevant.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Why did the regulatory impact statement cite the 2011 New Zealand
Institute of Economic Research report and table 1 as showing that the convention centre
would employ 500 full-time equivalents, when, in fact, no such figures are in either the
tables or the report from the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research 2011 report?
4 Sep 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 13231

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I would have to go back and check the comments the
member makes in relation to the regulatory imp act statement, but it is important for her
to realise that the figures referred to in the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research
report are a different se t of figures and do not bear any di rect relationship to the figures
around construction and operation of the conventi on centre. They are only an input into
the New Zealand Institute of Economic Resear ch report. The New Zealand Institute of
Economic Research report looks at wider ec onomic analysis and does not refer to the
number of jobs either in the construction or, in fact, in the operation of the centre.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: What discussion has he or his officials had with Skycity about its
participation or non-particip ation in the select committ ee process on the New Zealand
International Convention Centre Bill?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I had one conversation with the chair of Skycity on a
number of matters, including some not rela ted to Skycity. He asked whether it was
something that Skycity should do, and I said to  him that it was ope n to the company to
decide what to do. I did not think it was part icularly necessary, but  it was very much
Skycity’s call to make and I think it made its own call.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Can the Minister confirm that when his colleagues, such as Peseta
Sam Lotu-Iiga, voted in support of the Skyc ity deal, they did so on the basis of
incomplete and inaccurate financial analysis , inaccurate advice on the actual cost to the
taxpayer from this deal, incorrect projecti ons of job numbers, and a patently untrue
account of the impact of harm minimisation measures?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: No, the member is wrong on al l three of those counts. This
particular convention centre, which all of  the National Party caucus campaigned on at
the last election—and I appreciate  that this is the second time  in 2 days that the Green
Party has advised us not to follow the policies on which we were elected—will create
1,000 jobs in construction, will create 500 j obs in ongoing operation, and will enhance
the New Zealand convention industry. It is  a good deal for New Zealand, and this
Government believes strongly in it.
Businesses—Competitiveness and Financial Support from Government
2. Hon DAVID PARKER (Labour)  to the Minister of Finance: Does he stand by
his statement that “our companies are becoming more competitive”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes. I am pleased the member asked
that question, because this morning the Global Competitiveness Index for 2013-2014
was released. This shows that New Zealand has risen five places in the last year to a
ranking of 18. This is the first time New Zealand has placed ahead of Australia, which
has slipped back to 21 st place. New Zealand was ranked first in the world in the
following measures: procedures to start a busin ess, days to start a business, investor
protection, and inflation. We are ranked s econd in the world for soundness of its banks
and for trade barriers. We also ranked highly for health, education, quality of
institutions, goods, and labour market effici ency. Of course, there were other areas
where New Zealand was ranked lower, and we will, of course, move to improve those
rankings.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: How does intervening to override the determination of the
independent Commerce Commission for th e benefit of one company, Chorus,
demonstrate his Government’s commitment to  competitive and fair markets, given that
it will increase both fibre and copper broadband prices and reduce competition?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I disagree with most of what the member said. As the
member will know, the issues around Chorus  and fibre pricing are to do with the
Government’s project to roll out ultra-fast broadband, a project that was fully supported,
as I understand it, by the Oppositi on. Of course it represents a Government intervention
13232 Questions for Oral Answer 4 Sep 2013
in the market. That is the point of it, because  we believe that the market would not have
delivered ultra-fast broadband to most Ne w Zealand households probably for another
decade.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Does he support the effort of the Minister for Communications
and Information Technology to set the price for copper-based broadband at higher levels
than recommended by the Commerce Commission?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I do support the measures that the Minister for
Communications and Informa tion Technology is taking. As the member will know, at
some stage the country will have to pay the price of a new ultra-fast broadband
infrastructure. This Government decided that that time is now, not in 10 years’ time.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: What alternative policies has he seen that would affect the
competitiveness of New Zealand businesses?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The fact that New Zealand is rising in the ratings of
competitiveness but still has some way to go to get from No. 18 to No. 1 means we
should look out very carefully for policies that are going to hol d that progress back,
because a more competitive economy deliver s more jobs and, in particular, higher
incomes. I have seen proposals for a capital gains tax on every business and farm,
increasing emissions trading scheme taxes, minimum wage increases up to $18 an hour,
the cancellation of the 90-day trial peri od, winding back of ACC changes, extra
transport charges, and proposals to borrow a lot more money. These are all coming from
the Labour leadership campaign.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Does he believe Chorus and its competitors are being treated in
an even-handed manner by this Government, gi ven that Chorus alre ady has a 14 year,
$1 billion interest-free loan subsidised by the taxpayer, an d that other companies that
tendered for the ultra-fast broadband contract  could not get a base price for copper that
it is now giving to Chorus?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government’s programme to roll out ultra-fast
broadband roughly 10 years ahead of when it wo uld have occurred has been completely
transparent. We spent a good couple of years discussing with market participants the
process that we would follow. We went through a fully transparent, completely
commercial process, the result of which was th at Chorus and others won the contract to
roll out ultra-fast broadband. The Government  makes no apology for intervening in that
market to bring forward the roll-out of that network. Until today, I thought the Labour
Opposition supported that. It is now clear that  along with its policy of wanting to close
the smelter, it wants to stop the roll-out of ultra-fast broadband.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Could the Minister tell us  how many subcontractors are
about to go belly up because Transfield Serv ices, which is associated with the much-
vaunted ultra-fast broadband programme about  which he speaks, is not paying out and
is months behind in its payments?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Why can the Minister not unders tand that with the Rio Tinto
subsidy, the revisions to the Chorus subsi dy, and the casino convention centre deal, the
Government is saying to business and investors that it is easier to get ahead in this
economy by grifting corporate welfare from the Government via private phone calls and
dinner with the Prime Minister than it is  to succeed as a smaller business using
innovation and creativity to compete in the market place?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The member is talking nonsen se. If there was no ultra-fast
broadband roll-out, if the smelter had clos ed, and if there was no convention centre,
those members would be saying: “Why aren’t  you a smart, interven tionist Government
like we would be?”. No one believes Labour with that kind of contradiction. He is
talking rubbish.
4 Sep 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 13233
Economic Growth—Progress
3. PAUL GOLDSMITH (National)  to the Minister of Finance : What progress is
the Government making in building a stronger economy that will support more jobs and
higher incomes, following the domestic r ecession which started in early 2008 well
before the global financial crisis?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government is making good
progress in rebuilding the ec onomy after the recession began in 2008, before the global
financial crisis. Back then unemployment st arted to rise and the Government faced a
decade of deficits as a result of the stew ardship of the last Government. This week
Treasury published its monthly Economic Indicators  for August, which confirmed a
number of positive trends in the economy.  Households and businesses are becoming
increasingly optimistic and consumers, in particular, are beginni ng to spend more as
their confidence lifts. Of course, toda y we had the ratings from the World
Competitiveness Index that indicate that Ne w Zealand is beginning the long crawl back
from the damage done by the previ ous Government, which reduced our
competitiveness.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What did Treasury’s latest monthly Economic Indicators say about
the outlook for the labour market?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Treasury has noted that there is a modest strengthening of
the labour market in the June quarter, and not ed that the household labour force survey
confirmed that the number of people employe d rose by 8,000. This was a particularly
positive outcome, following a large increase in the number of people employed in the
March quarter. That means that over the pa st 6 months an extra 46,000 New Zealanders
have been employed. Treasury notes that th e quarterly employment survey showed a
similar strengthening in the number of filled jo bs. Of course, it has not grown as fast as
we would like, but 46,000 jobs in 6 months is a pretty solid effort and we hope that the
economy will build on that in the next 6 months.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: In the light of the improving la bour market, what do the latest
indicators say about wage growth?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Total weekly gross earnings grew by 1.2 percent in the June
quarter, according to the quart erly employment survey. Th is took annual growth and
weekly gross earnings to 3.8 percent. This is relatively subdued nominal wage growth.
However, with annual inflation at only 0.7 percent, real annu al wage growth is similar
to the rate in the mid-2000s—that is, real incomes are about 3.1 percent higher over the
year. That is above the level of inflation. This wage growth and low inflation will
continue to boost Kiwi family incomes. Of c ourse, we would like to see more of it, and
the competitiveness index results today indicate there is the possibility—the
probability—of better increases in incomes in the future because we are becoming more
competitive.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What progress is being made in rebuilding Christchurch, after the
devastating earthquakes, and what contribution is this making to economic growth?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Today marks the third anni versary of the first large
earthquake. We want to acknowledge the courage and resilience shown by the people of
Christchurch and communities across Cant erbury. They are making very good progress
in what are still difficult circumstances in th e challenging task of rebuilding their lives
and their communities. The Government con tinues to back the rebuild and boosted its
commitment in the May Budget, from $13 b illion to $15 billion. We are also working
hard to progress anchor projec ts in the Christchurch central  business district, with the
first section of the Avon Rive r precinct opened recently. Of c ourse, there are still issues
that are frustrating both homeowners and co mmercial building owne rs, related to the
13234 Questions for Oral Answer 4 Sep 2013
complexity of insurance arrangements in Christchurch. The extra activity is reflecting in
economic statistics: the Canterbury economy grew 6.6 percent in the last 12 months—
well ahead of other regions.
Housing, Affordable—First-home Buyers, Mortgages, and Reserve Bank
Intervention
4. PHIL TWYFORD (Labour—Te Atat ū) to the Minister of Housing : Does he
agree with the New Zealand Herald  that “the Government’s latest response to the
problem of housing affordability is as ill-directed as it is insipid”?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: No—although that editorial on our
KiwiSaver and Welcome Home Loan cha nges was entitled “no silver bullet” on
housing—but I do agree that th e changes to these schemes ar e a small part of what is
required to address housing s upply and affordability. That is why the Government has
taken action, including three major bills before this Parliament. In respect of the
KiwiSaver changes, more help was going to Southland and helping people there to get a
home deposit than to Auckland, despite the fact that Auckland has got 15 times the
population and three times the average house pr ice. Our change in the price caps and
also in the income caps will reverse that . In respect of the Welcome Home Loan
changes, they will increase threefold the number of families that are able to get a first
home.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Does he think Kiwis will find it easier or harder to get a first home
since the Government failed to secure an exemption for first-home buyers from loan-to-
value ratio lending limits, and since the ANZ, the ASB, the BNZ, and Westpac have all
put up their interest rates and their charges as a result of loan-to-value ratio lending
limits?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I do agree with the member that the level of interest rates is
one of the most important factors that affect  housing affordability. That is why I am so
proud to be part of a Government that has th e lowest interest rate s in 50 years. I note
that in the entire time I ha ve been in Parliament inte rest rates have gone up under
Labour Governments and come down under National Governments. In respect of the
very specific question—whether the Rese rve Bank charges have resulted in an
exemption—indeed they have. The Reserve Bank has said that Welcome Home Loans
will be exempted from the loan-to-value ratio limits, and that is one of the reasons that
the Government has trebled the number of Welcome Home Loans.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Does he agree with the Minister of  Finance, who told the House that
the lack of an exemption for first-home buye rs was not the fault of the Government but
was, in fact, the responsibility of the Reserve Bank; if so, is he calling the Reserve Bank
Governor a liar, given that th e governor said that  the use of these tools by the Reserve
Bank was recently agreed in a memorandum of understanding with the Minister of
Finance? And if so, does he think that the Minister of Finance is  calling himself a liar
when he said that the memorandum signe d by the Government provides four new
measures for the Reserve Bank, including loan-to-value ratios?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The member shows an ignora nce of the Reserve Bank of
New Zealand Act—an Act that was passed by  the previous Government—that is, the
decisions of the Reserve Bank are independent  of the Government, and we respect that
independence. In respect of what the Reserv e Bank has said, I would draw his attention
to the fact that the single gr eatest factor that the Reserve Bank said we needed to move
on, in respect of housing, was supply, and part icularly land supply.  That is what the
Government is doing. What the member and the members opposite are doing is actually
trying to stop the Govern ment from freeing up land s upply and making houses more
affordable.
4 Sep 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 13235

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Is he concerned that  low to middle income first-home buyers are
going to be disadvantaged by loan-to-value lending limits, given the reported comments
of mortgage broker Sonya Reid, who says that banks will cherry-pick clients, with those
on high incomes and professional occupations likely to be preferred?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: As occurs on so many issues, we get contradictions
between different Labour members. The first time—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: —I heard it proposed that there should be loan-to-value
ratio limits was—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I have a point of order from the Hon Trevor Mallard.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Yesterday we traversed on so me pretty regu lar occasions
what responsibility that Mini ster has for Labour Party polic y, and we agreed there was
none. Describing it is not his responsibility.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I agree with the point of order that has been raised. I am going to
ask Phil Twyford to ask the question again, and then ask the Minister to answer it.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Thank you. Is he con cerned that low to middle income first-home
buyers are going to be disadvantaged by loan-to-value lending limits, given the reported
comments of mortgage broker Sonya Reid, who says that banks will cherry-pick clients,
with those on high incomes and professional occupations likely to be preferred?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The most important thing for low and middle income
buyers wanting to get into their first home is  actually the level of interest rates. The
level of interest rates was such that when Labour left office, the average Kiwi household
was paying $250 a week more in their interest payments. The steps that have been taken
by the Reserve Bank and the steps that have be en taken by this Government are to keep
interest rates low for longer. That is the be st way in which we can help both first home
and other homeowners.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: What action will the Government take to help first-home buyers who
have already paid a 10 percent deposit, but w ill not be able to complete their purchase
before the 6-month grace period for loan-to-value ratios ends, meaning that they will
have to stump up an extra $50,000 or more within the next 6 months?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The member is incorrect in tw o respects. The first is that
the Reserve Bank has actually put a limit on, and not prohibited, the number of low-
value deposits. The banks have said that they  are going to give prio rity to first-home
buyers. The second point, in asking what the Government has done: the Government
has trebled—trebled—the numb er of Welcome Home Loans that are exempted from
those Reserve Bank limits. That means thousands more—thousands more—first-home
buyers will have an opportunity to get into their first home.
Foundation Courses—Initiatives Targeting Young People and Beneficiaries
5. COLIN KING (National—Kaik ōura) to the Minister for Tertiary Education,

items.speaker: Skills and Employment
items.text: What recent announcements has the Government made about
foundation education?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for T ertiary Education, Skills and
Employment): This morning I announced a num ber of changes to foundation
education—firstly, that the very successful Youth Guarantee scheme will be expanded
to 18 and 19-year-olds next year. It is curr ently available only to  16 and 17-year-olds,
with limited exceptions. The Youth Guarantee has been very successful in encouraging
16 and 17-year-olds to stay engaged in e ducation and to complete level 1 and 2
qualifications instead of dropping out and goi ng on to a benefit. However, there are
older teenagers aged 18 and 19 who have  already dropped out of school or who
otherwise need a chance to get that vital first level 2 qualification. With Youth
13236 Questions for Oral Answer 4 Sep 2013
Guarantee, trades academies, and the new vocational pathways, the Government is
confident that every single teenage New Z ealander has a fees-fre e path to a level 2
qualification, giving them access to training and skills for employment.

items.speaker: Colin King
items.text: What announcements has he made regarding training for beneficiaries?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: This morning, alongside the Minister for Social
Development, we announced that from next year the Government will be winding down
the Foundation-Focused Training Opportunitie s programme and replacing it with an
expanded range of effective education and training programmes to help beneficiaries
and young people get into work. From next year there will be considerably more places
at English for speakers of other languages cour ses, more places at intensive literacy and
numeracy courses, and more money spent on short courses that assist in getting
beneficiaries into work, and all New Zeala nders below the age of 25 will be able to
access fees-free level 1 and 2 courses.

items.speaker: Colin King
items.text: What announcements has he made about foundation education for 20 to
24-year-olds?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: This one is also very signifi cant. Starting from next year,
all level 1 and 2 foundation education course s will be fees-free for 20 to 24-year-olds.
Level 1 and 2 courses deliver core foundationa l skills required for success in life. They
provide students with the skills requi red for higher-level study, training, and
employment. Most students gain these skills and qualifications in a school setting, but
too many New Zealanders do not have these skills at age 20 and older. The changes I
have announced today mean that anybody under the age of 25 will be able to obtain a
level 2 qualification fees-free, whether that  is at a secondary school, through a Youth
Guarantee programme, or at a tertiary provider such as a private training establishment.
This is a very significant commitment to New Zealand’s future.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: What does the Minister say to the most high-risk unemployed
people in Dunedin about t oday’s announcement of the closure of the Foundation-
Focused Training Opportunities programme and the withdrawal of around $1 million
from trusted Dunedin second-chance e ducation providers such as the K ōkiri training
centre, the Dunedin Training Centre, th e Salvation Army, Approach Community
Learning, and Tokomairiro Training; and will the Minister guarantee that all of the
funding withdrawn by the Tertiary Educa tion Commission from Otago and Southland
will be reallocated through the Otago and Southland Work and Income offices?

8. CLAUDETTE HAUITI (National) to the Minister of Justice: What changes are

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: As a result of this Government’s

pre-sentence restorative justice conferences. In 2014-15 an additional 2,400 conferences
will be provided, bringing the total number of pre-sentence restorative justice

every court across New Zealand. To ensure providers are equippe d, the Ministry of

restorative justice helps to reduce reoffending and gives vic tims a stronger voice in the
justice system.

items.text: How do restorative justice conf erences contribute to positive
outcomes?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Restorative justice gives vic tims the ability to confront
their offenders and to tell them directly the impact their offending has had. It can be life
changing for both the victim, who is able to  express their feelings to the person who
caused their grief, and the offender, who is di rectly confronted with the results of their
actions. It is a voluntary  process, and both partie s have to agree to par ticipate. It is very
carefully supported by trained providers contract ed by the Ministry of Justice. Research
shows that 74 percent of victims who engage d in a conference felt safer and 80 percent
would recommend the process to  others. Research also sh ows a 20 percent reduction in

restorative justice conference.

This is fundamentally important, because  it is going to fund the National War
Memorial.”—the National War Memorial. The Future Investment—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: The “Future Fraud Fund”.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: The “Future Fraud Fund”—well, that might be right. It is a
slush fund. It is a political slogan that they trot out to try to justify this unpopular policy,
which is so unpopular that more than 300,000 New Zealanders have independently
signed a form saying: “Please don’t do this . Hold a referendum.”, and what is the
Government doing? It is ignoring it. Having spent hundreds of millions of dollars on the
asset sale process—hundreds of millions of dollars on the asset sale process—it says
that it is irresponsible of the Oppositi on parties to cause a referendum, where New
Zealanders are exercising their constitutional right to try and tell the Government that
they do not want it.
This Government has tried to hide from the New Zealand public the true effects of
this. At the time of the last election, it denied that its Budget went backwards by $100
million per annum. It had booked the proceeds of sale. It did not take any account of the
loss of revenue it suffers as a cost of a loss of profit shares.
4 Sep 2013 General Debate 13245
This Government’s economic programme is failing. We have got rampant house
price inflation, we have had more than 200,000 people go to Australia, and we have got
decline in the provinces because the economic promises of this Government are not
being made good.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: If there is a moment of truth
about asset sales, it will be the three La bour candidates out on the road campaigning for
the leadership, because they make one simple , effective promise: that they will borrow
$5 billion to $7 billion from foreign bankers and buy the Government shares back—that
they can buy them back. That is the true test of  leadership. I think that they will fail that
test. I do not believe for a moment that Da vid Parker believes what he said. What
Labour is hoping is that Nati onal will complete the asset sa les, so that Labour members
do not have to go out and say “We will borrow $5 billion to $7 billion from foreign
bankers to fulfil all the nutty promises our  leaders are making out on the campaign
trail.”
The fact that that is the issue today tells you that Labour has not had a new idea since
1994, when Mike Moore left the leadership. I have listened a little bit—as much as I can
stand it—to the three leadership candidates out  there. What it tells us is that the cream
of Labour’s crop is stale, completely uni maginative, and utterl y disconnected from
economic reality.
The worst bit of it is the complacency. La bour Party members believe that National
has done such a good job of ge tting the economy back on its feet that they can now go,
like a P-crazed Santa Claus, throwing lollies to the natives. That is what their leadership
candidates are doing. They clearly believe that all of the hard work has been done. They
clearly believe that now that we are going up the competitiveness rankings, and now
that we are ahead of Australia, we can put  our feet up as a country and go on a lolly
scramble. Well, they are wrong.
What it shows is they do not understand what has happened in this economy in the
last 6 or 7 years. They do not understand how hard normal working New Zealanders
have had to try to adapt to a changing world—to change the way their households work,
the way their workplaces work, and the way their lives work—so th at they can have
more jobs and better incomes.
The list of promises from the Labour candi dates looks like some kind of leftovers
from their candidate selection in the seat  of Sydenham in the mid-1960s, except they
have got some new words. They are “smart , regional, innovative,  strategic planning
partnerships”—whatever they  are—“with local government”.  It just goes on and on.
The main feature of it is that they now belie ve they can legislate wealth and incomes in
New Zealand. Cheap houses by legislation, ch eap electricity by le gislation, and higher
incomes by legislation.
The people in those audiences know, I think, that that is a hoa x. They would like to
think that that could be the way it is, and they like to see these fresh-faced, young, keen
prospective Labour leaders, Cunliffe and Robertson. They like to think that those young
men aspire to just pass a law to make us all wealthier. But in the back of their minds,
they are thinking “That chap Jones— he’s better than I thought.” That Woman’s Weekly
reader—he knows what happens in the real wo rld, while the rest of them are reading
Fabian Society monographs, repeating leftovers from the 1930s Communist Party in the
UK. Shane Jones is the dark horse coming th rough, and I hope he does because he has
got a few ideas.
The other striking thing about that contest is that nothing is being said about social
policy. The reforming Labour Party, the soci ally aware carers in the Labour Party—and
their leadership contestants have nothing to say about health, education, welfare, or
justice. The reason is that this Governme nt is doing such a good job of changing our
13246 General Debate 4 Sep 2013
social policy and the lives of disadvantaged New Zealanders for the better that Labour
Party members cannot even bring themselves to  criticise it. Even if they have no new
ideas and even if they are still peddli ng 1960s policies, could their leadership
contenders at least bother criticising National’s social policy?

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: That speech almost made Nick Smith
look stable. Can I say this: that Minister of Finance is the Minister who proves he could
not run a bath, let alone a State-owned ente rprise. Under that Minister’s watch, Solid
Energy, an export award - winning company, wa s driven into the ground because that
Minister went to sleep at the wheel and it is costing New Zealanders in excess of $350
million. Then we get to the T īwai deal. Mr English stood up yesterday, on Radio New
Zealand with Kathryn Ryan, and keeps saying ev ery day that the grea t deal he did with
Tīwai—a multibillion-dollar company. He halves its notice period, it gets cheaper
electricity, and then, just because he is  Santa Claus—talk about us taxing and
spending—he lobs in another 30 million bucks just to make it feel warm and cosy, of
course, after the billion-dollar profits it makes.  And then he says to us all: “The reason
we had to do this was we had to protect the jobs in Invercargill and Tīwai.”
Then he got caught with hi s trousers around his political ankles by Kathryn Ryan,
when she asked him: “Did you get a guarantee for T īwai? Did you get a guarantee that
they will keep every job, up until 1 January 201 7?”. The answer, in that sort of laconic
Southland lilt, was “No.” The second que stion: “Did you bother to ask for a
guarantee?”. Again, in that swede-like Southland fashion, he said “No.” He did not even
have the gumption, but he was honest enough at  that point to tell New Zealanders, to
even ask Rio Tinto: “Boys, would you hang on to the jobs at least until 1 January
2017?”. What he also knew was that before th e ink was dry on the deal on the Tuesday,
it was already sacking maintenance workers, a nd that is a fact in the media. It was
already announcing restructuring.

items.speaker: I say to that Minister of  Finance
items.text: “What a legacy.” Solid Energy—could not do
anything, would not do anything; just le t it all happen. There was $123 million of
bonuses, not to the boys in the coal-pit. Oh no. It went to the white-collar fellers who
actually ran the company into the ground. Then , of course, on asset sales, trumpeting
the Future Investment Fund, we find out, afte r the Prime Minister makes it up, that, oh
no, it is not going to hospitals and schools.  The $100 million allocated, which the poor
old Prime Minister did not even know he ha d signed off in his Budget—$100 million to
Solid Energy to bail it out.
And then we find the other little gift that  was thrown in. Where is the money coming
from, we found out, for the Mighty River Po wer free shares? Oh, out of the Future
Investment Fund. So there is $100 million, ther e is another $40 million, from the slush
fund, and a couple of other l ittle doozies—things like “str engthening capability on
security and risk management”. God help us, if anybody needed to do that, that mob
does, but it should not come out of the Futu re Investment Fund. Th en there is another
one: “Analysis of outcomes, Cabinet investment function”. I do not know what that
means, but it sounds quite trendy. But what doe s it come out of? The Future Investment
Fund. Not a hospital, not a school, not a bri dge, not a roadway. I will tell you what, Mr
English, you never have the guts to tell that to the people of New Zealand—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: When that Minister said  he was going to sell off—
[Interruption] Oh no, he did not. He never said it was going to go for free shares. He
never said it was going to go to bail out Solid Energy. We all remember the photo of
that member, with the platinum-plated spade,  at the briquette plant down in Southland,
saying how wonderful it was, as  he let the bonuses be paid ou t. This is the same plant,
of course, that Mark Ford is having to cl ose down and sack workers from. Oh, he was
4 Sep 2013 General Debate 13247
very proud there. He was a lion in his c onstituency—a lion—but he and old Liberace,
his Minister for State Owned Enterprises,  of course said: “O h no, nothing we will do.
We will not intervene.” But when it came to Meridian Energy, of course—

items.speaker: Hon Chester Borrows
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER

unparliamentary language: once in reference to  the Hon Bill English, accusing him of
being untruthful, and, secondly, when he referred to a member over here as Liberace.

items.text: Order! I have heard enough. The me mber did not use the word I

items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.text: Is this a fresh point of order?

items.text: Yes, it is. It was not the word “lion”. It was further back in
his speech when he related comments made  by the Hon Bill Eng lish, and it was not the
word “lion”. I was not confused by that word.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I am unsure what the word was, but the member to whom it was
directed certainly did not take  any offence. I think he was quite enjoying the debate. It
was a robust debate, and this is the general debate. The member can carry on.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: I do not know what the Minister for Courts was
chewing. It might have been some sort of  medication, or whatever, I do not know, but
obviously it has got to him. The point here, despite all the silly points of order because
they want to hide this away, is that the Minister of Finance went to the country on a
spurious claim, saying that he would se ll assets to buy other assets—sell revenue-
generating assets, of course, to buy non - reve nue-generating assets. He never told the
people of New Zealand that the slush fund would be used for $140 million—$100
million to Solid Energy to bail out his mess-up, and $40 million for the free shares.
Now we have got Meridian Energy—you know, buy now, pay later, get a set of steak
knives. That boy should be on “As Seen On TV”—the Shopping Channel. He would
sell anything. He made it up. He was not hone st with the people of  New Zealand. He
should pull the pin and allow the people to have their say through a referendum.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Yesterday I had delight and pride
in publishing these infographics on the New Zealand Education Profile. But what
question do we get today from the Opposition? A pathetic question on the integration of
Wanganui Collegiate School, which happened ove r 8 months ago, and that is all that
Opposition members can talk about. What this  infographic shows in one sheet is the
distinction between this Government and the Opposition and the three contenders for
the leadership out there. First of all, we are aspirational. We want five out of five kids to
be successful, yet in the entire 9 years of  that administration, those members were
happy to wring their hands over one out of five kids being failed by our system, yet they
were going out and telling their traditional roots how committed they were to them. In 9
years they made not a dint of effort or di fference to those people. This Government, in
the 5 years we have been in office, has tackled the hard questions. We are aspirational.
Another distinction is that we are accountab le. We are prepared to say what we are
going to do, which is to ensure that 85 percent of 18-year-olds should have the
minimum qualification so that they can participate in the labour market, so that they can
earn the incomes they want for their own home s, and so that they are independent of
government. This is all completely opposite to what the Opposition wants. It wants
unhappy, undereducated, aggrieved, dependent people, because that is whom it relies on
in order for it to suck votes out of people who deserve better. We are giving them better.
13248 General Debate 4 Sep 2013
We are transparent. We report on what we are trying to do. We identify the
challenges still ahead of us, and they are significant. Although on average four out of
five kids are being successful, and that is great and we want them  to do better, that
masks another picture, where there are t oo many young people who are still failing, and
too many of those are M āori and Pasifika, have special education needs, or come from
poorer homes. This Government is dedicated to delivering to all of them.
We are detailed. We know how many boys, how many girls, what ethnicity, and in
what part of the country, because the more  precise we can be, the more targeted and
responsible we can be with taxpayers’ money. We are not a lolly scramble Government,
unlike the members on the Opposition side, who are out and about across the country
promising things that they have no costi ngs for and, indeed, have no policy framework
for, let alone a budget. We are committed to  a world-class education system, and we
know that one of the characteristics of that is a data-rich environment. We know that the
ability to operate effectively—with what the evidence tells us—will be important for
raising the educational status of every one of our New Zealand children.
Each of the three Labour members who are out there auditioning to become the next
leader of the Labour Party got a great edu cation—each and every one of them. Is there
one promise they have made about education?  Not at all. Have they mentioned it all?
Not once. No, they talked about full employment—yes, full employment requires
skilled, qualified young people. That is the big step that the Opposition has not fully
understood. This side of the House has, and we  are dedicated to it. It is committed to a
Pasifika television channel, but not to Pasifika education. We, too, are committed to the
culture, the language, a nd the identity of th e wonderfully diverse Pasifika community
that is contributing to this country. But guess what? Their contribution to themselves,
their own aiga, and their communities is going to be stronger on the back of a good
education. That is what we are committed to, long before we get a television channel.
What else have Labour members promised to do? Well, they have promised a 50
percent female quota for caucus, but they ha ve not looked at how well girls are doing in
our education system. They have promised not  to block the man ban if the party wants
it, but they have not focused on what we need to do for boys in education, and for
brown boys in particular, which our system has not yet proved it is able to deliver to.
So, yes, we have got Labour-lite leaders ou t there talking, and ta lking, and talking,
based on having had an excellent  education themselves, but there is not one word and
not one commitment to education for New Zealanders.
This Government puts its money where its mouth is. We have put $9.7 billion into
Vote Education this year. That is a 74 pe rcent increase on early childhood education,
and a 30 percent increase on schooling. This Opposition has talked about the closures of
schools by this Government. Well, let me—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member’s time has expired.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: This country has a most serious
situation on its hands. Once more a top security agency has acted illegally, and it is time
for the Prime Minister and the Minister of Fore ign Affairs to front. In July last year the
Fijian military dictatorship contacted th e New Zealand Government regarding the
freedom and democracy movement. Some ki nd of deal was struck. The Security
Intelligence Service and police raided a hous e in Auckland where former Fiji Cabinet
Minister Rajesh Singh was living. The SIS o fficer refused to produc e a search warrant.
They took a computer and a cellphone, and, by some strange coincidence that only the
Prime Minister cannot explain, a Fijian military officer sent a text to the former Cabinet
Minister subject to the raid that showed that he knew the SIS was raiding that place—
his place—at that very time. In short, th e Fiji military knew the SIS was raiding an
Auckland property.
4 Sep 2013 General Debate 13249
There were other texts a couple of days la ter. They were chil ling, and I want to
repeat them exactly as they came. This is from the same person in Fiji: “Hmm … yeah
all over Fiji news … Fiji One … your name and picture came up … we telling Fiji
One”—this is actually as he wrote it—“did  they get facts tight according to media
decree … cause you can sue them …”.

items.speaker: Another text
items.text: “… don’t know why Fiji tarnish ur name. Don’t worry we defend you.”

items.speaker: Third one
items.text: “Yes, media”—

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: This is more confusing than usual.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: It is not confusing, because it is evidence, for his
sake. The third text: “Yes, media have bran ded u as terrorist. There is word you could
be deported.” Text No. 4: “Fiji-NZ  Talks—-Foreign Affairs Minister R ātū Kubuabola
has met in suva with his New Zealand counterpart Murray McCully to discuss
rebuilding diplomatic relations between the countries. NZ, Fiji holding positive talks—
Fiji and New Zealand have held talks to rebuild diplomatic relations.”

items.speaker: The fifth one
items.text: “Bro you not worth a bulle t cause u don’t deserve it.” It goes on to
say—and the sixth, the seventh, and the eighth texts are all of the same tenor—“Don’t
worry about us … u becoming a thorn in NZ  govt … ”. No. 9: “Reality check bro … u
the culprit now … NZ [Foreign Affairs Minister] met ours in suva last week … hmm.”
Then there is No. 10 and No. 11, but No. 12 is  the one: “Bro, terrorist? We did raid
you,”—do you hear this? It says: “We did ra id you, it was NZ SS, so ask them …”
Then, going on to No. 13, wher e the guy is alleging he is a terrorist in the text—and he
goes on to say this here, in No. 14: “NZ SIS raid Rajesh Singh house for plotting to
[assassinate] Fiji PM. Well you will be deported soon for being threat to the NZ govt.”
No. 15: “That’s a process of restoration of democracy … nz is funding … so any
unnecessary comments from you in NZ will be treated as impeding this process … so
NZ will [be] informed … hehehe … pliz  don’t disturb my mtg with my NZ
counterpart.” No. 16, the last text, says: “I don’t talk to terrorist … as branded by nz
govt …”.
That is all evidence of the knowledge of the Fijian Government before the raid
happened, as the raid happened, and after the raid happened. This is a military
dictatorship that this Gove rnment is cuckolding our country with. The texts leave no
doubt that the Fiji dictatorship knew what was happening and that the Fiji military had
contacts in high places in New Zealand. I want to know how far the SIS was involved,
and what on earth is the Prime Minister doing parked up there in Majuro in the Marshall
Islands, shouting out to somebody in this  Parliament—who has got the facts and
evidence, which I will table to the media—to put up or shut up. It is time for him to put
down the mai tais in Majuro and to stop acting as some potentate with his feet above the
heads of other people, to start acting like a Prime Minister, and to get back to this
country and tell us why he has got the Fijians  involved in conspiracies to break the law
in our country with the SIS and Government Communications Security Bureau as well.
Why did the Government drop its defence over this matter, and a court case, when
one of the participants sued the Minister of Internal Affairs when he took action? It got
to within a week of the cour t case and the Department of Internal Affairs dropped its
defence because it knew that the illegal SI S involvement was about to come out. Why
did the inspector-general throw out Mr Singh’ s complaint? He talked to the police.
What happened? Nothing. Only the Ombudsman showed any sympathy. Nothing has
happened against the agencies or the Mini sters involved. This raises even more
questions. To close, it is time for answers, and we will get them.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: The Dominion Post the other day had the headline
“Rivals’ policies out of touch, out of time”—out of touch and out of time. That really
does sum it up. I want to talk about Shane J ones, who I actually think should be the
13250 General Debate 4 Sep 2013
leader of the Labour Party, be cause at least he has got a few ideas. He has got a few
ideas. You know, he knows how to  talk the language of the everyday New Zealander,
the Joe and Mary Bloggs out there. But guess what? I am appalled by what is happening
in the Labour Party, because we have got David Cunliffe, supported by Louisa Wall and
Nanaia Mahuta; we have got Grant Robert son—I will talk about Grant Robertson’s
little cameo on TV the other night very shortly—supported by Moana Mackey and by
Meka Whaitiri; and then we have got poor old Shane, supported by only Rino.
You know, for the first time in  the party’s history, tangata  whenua has put his hand
up and said: “I would like to be the leader of one of New Zeala nd’s major parties. I
would like to be the leader.” You would ha ve thought that this was the opportunity for
Labour to grab the M āori vote back from the M āori Party and grab the M āori vote back
from the Mana Party in the north and say that it is speaking the language of the M āori
electorate and that that is why it has a M āori leader of the Labour  Party, and actually
one who has a few clues about where the battle  will be won. As sure as hell it will not
be won out on the extreme left, where Mr Cunliffe and Mr Robertson are pushing
themselves because they want to be with their mates over here, the Green Party.
I saw something the other night. I was absolutely gobsmacked. People do not want to
talk about it. Here was Grant Robertson on TV  being asked by the interviewer: “Where
is your partner?”. Grant Robertson said, as bold as Larry: “Oh, he’s not here. He’s got
something else to do.” But roll back the vi deotape and you can see that Alf was behind
him, wandering past, over to another table. Why would you do that? Why would you lie
in front of national TV? He must be embarrassed. I do not know. I do not know. The
fact of the matter is that what we have seen  is one of the candida tes telling a bold-faced
lie on national TV. He wants to represent this country. That says to this country that it is
OK to lie on national TV and not even apologise for it.
A day later, 2 days later, questions have  been asked in the Twitter world about why
he said that. I never thought that Grant was a liar, until I saw that video clip. It sends a
message. It sends a—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: You’re wrong.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Am I wrong? Oh, I am wrong. O h, I am wrong. It must have
been computer-generated imagery. It must have been computer-generated imagery, the
way they put Alf in the pictur e. Poor old Grant did not ev en know that hi s partner was
behind him, even though 5 seconds before th at he was having a beer with him. And
even when he was asked about it, they both smiled at each other. Oh no, that smile was
computer-generated imagery as well.
I have got news for the Labour Party, and I am afraid that it is all bad. Labour
members have been running around saying wh at a great election campaign it has been.
Two hundred people turned up—200 people—to a meeting to elect the leader of the
Labour Party. For goodness’ sake! And I tell you what, I saw it on Te Karere and I
recognised some of these people. Some of those people have been in more parties than I
have, and that is saying something. For goodness’ sake!
It has been great, but I tell you what, I want to finish by saying that the last speech
made by the Rt Hon Winston Peters is a sad indictment on how things have really,
really got out of hand for that old chap. Thinking of and believing in conspiracies is just
wrong.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. I think you heard the reference to the right honourable member, who should be
addressed in that way and not in the way that the member just did.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Yes, I accept the point. The memb er has now finished his speech,
