4 Sep 2013 General Debate 13251

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: It is 4 September today, and for those
of us from Canterbury it  is time for us to recall that on this day 3 years ago we started
our series of very significant earthquakes. For the rest of the country, I think most
people think “I wish you’d ge t over it.”, but, actually, as  I think Wellingtonians are
starting to understand, it is not the quakes that have the hu ge impact on people; it is
dealing with the bureaucracy. That has been the hardest part. I have a friend who has a

items.speaker: T-shirt that says on the front
items.text: “I survived  10,000-plus quakes.”, and on the back it says
“But dealing with EQC and IAG is killing me.”  Actually, quite literally, that is the case
for so many people. I want to acknowledge  the citizens of Canterbury, the emergency
services, the military, our social services, our health care workers, and our community
leaders. They have been extraordinary througho ut a very, very long and hard 3 years. I
know also that for many this 3-year annivers ary today triggers th e hardest and saddest
of memories for many people in Canterbury.
It was not just the people of Canterbury who responded so well in the initial period
after both our September and February qua kes—looking after each other, even letting
cars in ahead of you in traffic, which, as you will know, Mr Speaker, is an extraordinary
occurrence in Canterbury—the way that peopl e in our towns and cities throughout New
Zealand, and actually intern ationally, responded was overw helming. The outpouring of
support for us was huge, and it was greatly ap preciated. It came from many people who
could barely afford to support themselves, but they were so ge nerous that they
supported us in our hour of need.
The Prime Minister came to Christchurch an d he said to people in one of the most
broken suburbs that nobody would be worse off in Christchurch as a result of these
quakes. Those words had huge significance for people. People cl ung on to that as a
commitment from the Government that nobody  would be worse off. On reflection, I
think it was a poorly chosen phrase to use when, I guess, not many people envisaged the
challenge ahead. But the Prime Minister did say that, and people clung to that
throughout a lot of hard times.
One of the areas where people are worse off is with the offer that the Government
has made to people who are in the red zone who have bare land or commercial property.
The Government has offered those people in  the red zone 50 percent of the rating
valuation of their land—the 2007 rating valuat ion of their land. They took that offer to
court because they did not think it was fair, and the judge just last week came back and
said that that is true, that that is not a fair offer, and he told the Minister for Canterbury
Earthquake Recovery to go back to the drawi ng board and start again. He also said that
the zoning, which has caused such trauma for so many people, was done outside the
law. These are very big and significant issues for people.
The Prime Minister was then confront ed by media about Justice Panckhurst’s
decision overturning the 50 percent bare land offer a nd the zoning, and noting the
zoning as being made outside the law. The Prime Minister said: “Oh, well, we could
just walk away. We could say that it has been a bit of f un but now we are over it, and
the Government could walk away.” That expression—the Prime Minister saying to
Cantabrians that the Government might walk away and saying that “It’s been a bit of
fun.”—was one of the most in sensitive, hurtful, and, actually, cruel comments that he
could have made, because it has not been fun fo r any of us. If anyone thinks that we are
bleating, they are wrong. It certainly has not been fun.
In the paper this morning Kendra Street was quoted. She said: “I am cold. I am tired.
I am frustrated. My government has forgotte n me and my insurance company is slower
than snails racing through peanut butter.” And she does not speak alone. She said: “This
is not what I wanted for my child. But it is  what he got. I cannot blame mother nature—
we survived the earthquakes. It is our govern ment and our insurance company’s lack of
13252 General Debate 4 Sep 2013
empathy, and stalling, stalling, st alling that keep us in this stress.” What she said is
“What I want is a warm house to live in. What I want is my child to not be afraid of [our
arguments or] the dark … I want to not fight with my husband about money, the
insurance, and when to turn the heater on.” Kendra Street said: “I want my life back.”
Her son was just 22 months old. He is now nearly ready to start school. The difference
is that in the first quake her son was 22 months old, and now he is about to go to
school—there is no progress. It is time for the Government to step up and help.

items.speaker: KATRINA SHANKS
items.text: It is my pleasure to take a call in this general
debate today. On 15 September the weird and wacky reality TV show has its finale, and
a new leader of the Labour Party will emer ge. Not only that but we have only 11 more
episodes of this TV show to go.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Has this member ever won an election?

items.speaker: KATRINA SHANKS
items.text: The question, Mr Mallard, is  whether contender Grant,
contender Shane, or contender David will be the winner of this contest. The question the
Labour caucus members are asking themselves is  when one of these contenders, Grant,
Shane, or David, does become the leader of the Labour Party—and they have been
going around creating these policies on the run, which they are going to have to stand
by in the 2014 election and which the caucus has not bought into, which the party has
not bought into, which they have not costed, and which they have not consulted on with
the sector—in 2014, when the caucus has to stand united behind this leader with
policies that the caucus has not bought into and has not discussed, what is going to
happen? I can tell you right now. The cau cus will not be united. There will be
infighting, and Labour will not be the Gove rnment in 2014. There is no way it possibly
can be, not when those contenders are maki ng policy on the run like this, by one person
in isolation.
It is really interesting when you look at these policies of contenders No. 1, No. 2, and
No. 3, because these policies do not reflect wh at New Zealanders are concerned about.
They do not reflect education. They do not ta lk about health care. They do not talk
about crime and law and order. They do not talk about job growth. They do not talk
about housing affordability. All the big issues that face New Zealand, contestants No. 1,
No. 2, and No. 3 do not even address. That  shows you how out of touch the Labour
Party is and how out of touch the potential leaders of this Labour Party will be.
We listen to and we read a nd we hear all the commentary from the contenders about
what these policies are going to look like, an d the one really interesting policy they all
have is creating wealth through legisl ation. How do you do that? How do you create
wealth through legislation?

items.speaker: Hon Chester Borrows
items.text: You can’t.

items.speaker: KATRINA SHANKS
items.text: You cannot. How do you create wealth? You create it
through companies. You crea te it through the companie s and their investing in
themselves, emerging companies going to markets, companies creating products that are
high tech and high value, then employing mo re people in high-growth areas in high-
growth jobs that pay a lot of money. That  is how you create wealth for a country, not
through legislation.
What are some of these policies? Well, w hy do I not start with Shane Jones? I like
his. He has got a couple of really good ones. I like it when he says: “I will not write one
single cheque the Labour Party cannot cash.” I believe in that. I believe that that is right.
You should not promise something you cannot deliver. But then he goes on to say,
unfortunately, that he will increase the minimum wage. I do not quite know how that is
going to flow out. He says he is going to give  tax incentives for businesses to invest in
the regions. Yes, we all want to grow businesses. We agree with that. But tax
4 Sep 2013 General Debate 13253
incentives—has he costed that out? I think maybe not. He is going to extend the rail link
to Northport.
The one thing I do really like about his policy is supporting mining. In his words,
“I’d rather have the young people of the north  with a shovel in their hand rather than
wandering around picking locks.” He says that  this should not be a shocking stance
from someone in the Labour Party, as it was born from mining. He said: “I want to see
little brown Kiwis staying at home and not going to Australi a. If that means offending
the Greens from time to time, such is life.” I will tell you what—tha t is about the most
sensible thing any of these potential leaders have said yet.
When I look over at the Labour caucus sitting opposite me, the members who are in
the House, none is engaged in this convers ation. None is jumping up and saying: “I
support this contender.” They are all silently sitting th ere, looking down, embarrassed,
knowing that the potential leader has committed that caucus to policies it has not bought
into. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: It may not realise it, but this Government has
ruled out New Zealand’s support for any military  action in Syria that is not authorised
by the United Nations Security Council. Let me read out to the House the Government’s
answer to my question on action over Syri a of 15 February 2012: “7. Dr Kennedy
Graham (Green) to the Minister of Foreign Af fairs: Will he give an assurance that New
Zealand’s armed forces will not be used in any possible military intervention in Syria in
violation of the United Nations Charter? Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman (Minister of
Defence) on behalf of the Minister of Fore ign Affairs: Yes. Dr Kennedy Graham: Is he
then, … in a position to confirm that the G overnment does not support external military
involvement in Syria unless it responds to a United National Security Council resolution
authorising it—that is to say, no coalition of the willi ng is legal without that mandate?

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: New Zealand alwa ys follows the United Nations Security
Council resolutions, so we would not be doing anything in violation of that.”
I congratulate the Government . Let me point out why it was so insightful 18 months
ago. Syria is a global human tragedy in a de fining moment in the modern struggle for
global peace and justice. There can be no la wful military action in Syria without proof
to the United National Security Council of  chemical weapon use and by whom. And
even if proof is provided, there can be no military action without authorisation by the
council. That is not a matter of political judgment; it is a non-negotiable legal
requirement. The US is advancing the argument that there is a legal justification based
on humanitarian intervention. Th at is incorrect. That doct rine, more appropriately
known today as responsibility to protect, does not trump the United Nations Charter.
That was made clear in United Nations Ge neral Assembly Resolution 60/1, paragraphs
138 and 139, in 2005. The US is being somewh at disingenuous here. Even if the UN
were to authorise military action, thereby ma king it legal, it would require a separate
decision on the part of each country as to  the political merit of becoming directly
involved. The doctrine lays down six criteria fo r such a judgment. The critical issue is
whether the action proposed would relieve sufferi ng rather than cause more. It is almost
certain it would not.
If we ever needed a lesson in caution, it was the illegal military action against Iraq by
the US, the UK, and Australia in 2003. The evidence adduced to the council as proof of
a nuclear weapon programme proved to be fa lse—indeed, part-fabrication. For its part,
the much maligned United Nations Security Council declined to agree to such an
invasion. That was not simply a French veto. A majority of the council opposed military
action, yet those three countries proceeded without UN authorisati on, and illegally. If,
in the case of Syria, the council chooses not  to act because of a veto, it does not mean
the council is dysfunctional a nd not doing its job. It means the council has decided not
13254 General Debate 4 Sep 2013
to act. The council would actually be doing its job, just as it did with Iraq in 2003. Many
in the West might resent that fact, retaining a 20 th century sense of mo ral and political
superiority. But they cannot disown the fact —indeed, they created it. They created the
UN, and they refuse to this day to change the charter when the prospect of doing so is
before them. They refuse to surrender or ev en circumscribe their veto, and then, when
they confront a situation, wh en another permanent member casts a veto, they seek to
circumvent that veto by acting around it. S o, if the US and the UK are concerned about
vetoes impeding Security Council action, they can rectify the situat ion by agreeing to
surrender the veto, or, at least, by agreeing to  its strict circumscription to only when
their vital interests of survival are at stake.  Let this Parliament have a chance to debate
this matter when it next meets.

items.speaker: PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.text: What an unedifying spectacle we have before us,
watching the three candidates from Labour —Cunliffe, Robertson, and Jones—crawling
all over each other to offer more to their mates. The unions will be happy, but the rest of
New Zealand will be wondering who is going to f oot the bill. It is a lolly scramble, said
John Armstrong in the New Zealand Herald this morning, and I found myself agreeing
with him.
So what are they going to do? They are going to immediately lift the minimum wage
to $15 an hour. Well, that is up 9 percent on the current minimum wage. On top of that,
the privileged Government workers—I have  not quite worked out why Government
workers need to be so much more privileged—are going to have their wages lifted up to
$18.40 an hour. That is a 34 percent increase on the minimum wage, tomorrow. Is that
not wonderful? That is up by a third. It is going up faster than the Auckland rates. Now
all you have to do is vote fo r Cunliffe and vote for Robe rtson and your wage magically
goes up by 34 percent. I wonder who amongst th em is going to commit that they would
reject any cascade of relati vity agreements about this. The people who are currently
earning $18.40 an hour will think “OK, well, it’s gone up so we should go up to $22.”,
and the people earning $22 an hour will think “Well, that’s not fair. Mine should go up
to $26.” And what about the Public Serv ice Association members working for the
Government who are earning $100,0 00 a year? They will be as king: “Well, theirs have
gone up 34 percent. Why shouldn’t mine go up 34 percent?”—and so on and so on.
Where will it end?
You have to go back to 1985 to see such a reckless inflationary piece of public policy
put on this country. I think it was Stan Rodger and David Lange—the lady there in
charge of the health policy in Labour thes e days, Annette King, was in Parliament back
then, and Phil Goff, but nobody else was arou nd since we have had such a reckless
inflationary piece of public policy put on the parchment as  what we are talking about
here. We expect it from Mr  Robertson. He is a public se ctor union man through and
through. He is all about spendi ng and redistributing money, not about earning it. But I
am surprised that we see it from Cunliffe, a man with some business experience.
David Cunliffe, the Quade Cooper of New Zealand politics, should know better. He
should know that you cannot pass off this kind of thing as costing $20 million, when we
know that it could be $2.5 bil lion, which is our expectation of the increase in minimum
wages if they are going to give everybody who happens to work for Parliament a
minimum wage of $18.40. Why would they do that? It is not as if we do not have very,
very generous redistribution arrangements with Working for Families so that anybody
on the minimum wage with dependent children in New Zealand receives credits rather
than tax and gets a significant boost from the rest of New Zealand.
It is very worrying watching this lolly scra mble that we are seei ng on the other side,
because it reflects a world where, by magic,  wages can be put up, and where, by magic,
Mr Jones can walk into the supermarket and reduce the cost of  food everywhere by
4 Sep 2013 General Debate 13255
dealing with the so-called duopolies. I do not want that man anywhere near my
chickens. It is all about pande ring to the entitlement culture that bedevils New Zealand.
This is the truth. New Zealand as a nation is not entitled to anything. We are not entitled
to any standard of living, other than what we go out and earn. We have to earn our way.
The Government must manage its finances, it must operate its Public Service in a way
that is focused on results, not just spend m oney for the sake of it, and it must focus on
building a more productive and competitive ec onomy. That is what National is doing,
and that is why it continues to enjoy such success and why it is making great progress to
get us back to surplus and to get this country growing effec tively—so much more
effectively than so many other countries in the OECD.
We are living in a golden age right now, not withstanding the terrible events in Syria
that the previous speaker, Dr Kennedy Gr aham, alluded to. When we look around our
region we see India and we see China growing; hundreds of millions of people are being
lifted out of poverty as we speak. They are looking for products. They are looking for
the sorts of things that New Zealand produces . This is a wonderful time to be living in
New Zealand and it is a very positive time for this country, but we have to grasp it. We
need to reward enterprise, we need to cel ebrate entrepreneurship, and we certainly do
not hear any of that from the Labour Part y. Instead we have a parade of dinosaurs
pandering to the insular, unrealistic, entitlem ent culture that is holding us back as a
country, and it is time we heard the end of it. Thank you.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: This Government is a two-trick
pony. It has only two things to sell: they are assets and the hope that the Christchurch
rebuild will stimulate our economy. This G overnment is a two-trick pony. I would line
up our three thoroughbreds any da y against that other side. They are doing a fantastic
job.
I would like to talk about a few things : Meridian Energy, Might y River Power, and
Tīwai Point. Those names will go down in hi story as the disaster that sunk this
Government. We have had some contributions this afternoon that have been absolutely
dreadful. Hekia Parata tried to say that this Government is detail conscious and that it is
accountable. It does not even know how much it is going to raise from the asset sale
programme. It is just a best guess—$5 m illion to $7 million. It does not even know
what it is going to raise. It does not know when it is going  to sell. It does not know how
it is going to sell it. It trie s to put out discounts  and carrots to the investing public. The
public of New Zealand know that they do not want these asset sales. We already own
these assets. The public of New Zealand know that they do not have the funds. There is
only a 3 percent uptake from retail investors fr om the float. Do you think that Meridian
Energy is going to achieve a wonderful bounce in the market? Absolutely not. It is the
wrong time to be selling, and New Zealanders  are telling the Gove rnment that through
their call for a referendum. Again, that is ju st one trick from the two-trick pony that is
an absolute disaster for this Government.
I would like to move on to Mr Tau Hena re, a whanaunga of mine from up in the
mighty Ngāpuhi, Ngāti Hine. Mr Henare said some di sgraceful things about lies being
said on TV. John Key lies to New Zealand ev ery single day. This Government lies to
New Zealand every single day. Tau Henare  was once a fine member of the Labour
whānau. He is old-school Labour. He has played every position. He has played every
position in the backline. He has played in Ne w Zealand First. He has played in Mauri
Pacific—what was that one? And now he is playing in the National Party. All I can say
to my whanaunga is “Come back to mother  ship Labour. Come back to mother ship
Labour, e hoa.”

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: No!
13256 General Debate 4 Sep 2013

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: No, that is all right. I retract that. I definitely retract that. I do
retract that.
Then we had dear Miss Katrina Shanks—a very, very nice lady—but she would have
to go down as the main contender for New Z ealand’s next worst politician. That was an
absolutely dreadful contribution from her. We know that Miss Shanks is a star on
YouTube. She is a star. She knows what being a contender is like. She actually topped
Miss South Carolina with her absolutely  intelligent debate s and thoughtful and
intellectually robust debates on informati on technology matters. That was a dreadful
contribution. But she is a very nice lady. Again, we will leave that as it is—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I wouldn’t go that far.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: OK, Mr Mallard, maybe not that  far. But getting back to my
debate, I go around my big electorate—it covers two-thirds of the land mass of
Aotearoa—so I get to go around and I talk to  a lot of people. The people whom I meet
are scared because not a month goes by—e specially when I have been down in
Invercargill, where we have seen a $30 million handout to Rio Tinto and to the
aluminium smelter at T īwai Point down there. But what has that given the people of
Southland? Sure, it has given them a slight reli ef, but there is uncertainty in the lives of
those people because they do not know what is round the corner. Rio Tinto could come
back in 2050 and it could play the Government in terms of this shocking deal that it has
bought into. That is a shocking deal.
I am going to go on to another matter because  I am short of time. I want to pay
tribute to the people of Chri stchurch, the heart of Te Tai Tonga. This is a very
significant day. It has been a real rough 3 years. I do think of all the resilient wh ānau
who have been working through these difficult times—many Māori whānau—especially
those with a lot of housing difficulties and troubles. We are sta nding by them. I know
that my colleagues are also doing a lot of work. I mihi to them on this day. Kia ora
tātou.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: Malo e lelei. It is Tongan Language Week, so I want
to acknowledge our Tongan community that are out there. In fact, I was honoured to be
here in the House on Monday, when we celebrated the launch of Tongan Language
Week. One of the thi ngs I talked about th en with our Tongan co mmunity was how they
ignited the Rugby World Cup. Wh at they did was gridlock Auckland Airport. There
were 4,000 or 5,000 Tongans—you talk to many of them and they say there were
20,000 Tongans—out there. There was a sea of red, a wave that was going on to
celebrate and ignite the world cup. It was great. The point of difference was this: it was
the use of cultural capital to make a difference.

items.speaker: Here is the interesting thing about that point
items.text: everybody wanted to own them. Labour
said: “Isn’t that great?”. Those member s looked at the colour and thought: “That
represents us.” But here is what we ar e now hearing from our Tongan community, and
also from our Māori community: “Has Labour taken us for granted?”. Has it taken them
for granted? The answer is, yes, it has.
Where is the evidence for this? Well, there is what Willie Jackson said. He may not
always be loved and liked by the Labour Party, but this is what  he said. He said that in
this contest of choosing a new leader, it wa s time that the Labour Party, which has for
80 years enjoyed the support of Māori, made a difference. It is time for Labour to put its
money where its mouth is and say: “Let’s elect a M āori leader”. Will it do it? No, it will
not.
What about Haare Williams, who is there in the Labour Party? He is the vice-
president for the M āori elect. He said that it is time for Labour to stand up and take
account. M āori have supported Labour for 80 l ong years, Mr Clark—80 long years.
Will Labour stand up? Will it take account? No, it will not.
4 Sep 2013 General Debate 13257
Why will it not? I will tell you the reasons why. Labour has taken Māori and Pasifika
for granted. Well, I tell you what, here is the writing on the wall, and it is not from us; it
is from your own. Josie Pagani on Q+A on Sunday, looking at the debate, said: “Labour
has lost touch, like what Shane Jones said, w ith the common people. It is about time we
went back to where we are from.”

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: They don’t like your casino deal. The Pasifika communities are
betrayed.

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont
items.text: How do you feel about having lost touch? You’ve lost touch.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: So here is the interesting th ing, Mr Clark, that you need to
listen to—and Mrs Beaumont. Here is the interesting thing that she said, and you have
got to take note of this: “Out of the 800,000 votes that we potentially have lost”—
because, remember, only 18 percent actually supported the Labour Party at the last
election. This is what was said  by Josie Pagani. She said the information that they have
and the surveys said that “they’re brow n, they’re young, and they’re living in the
regions.” She asked who, when you look at the three contestants, would best reflect the
leadership that the young, brow n, and in the regions could support. Guess what? It is
Shane Jones. But will Labour members support  him? No, they will not. No, they will
not. No, they will not.
Your time has come. The time has come when M āori and Pasifika—and let us take a
look at this. In 2005 Mike Williams, a former president of the Labour Party, said that
the only reason why Labour won that election was South Auckland Pasifika voters, who
came up, who showed up, and who put their money where their mouth was. But guess
what? You have taken them for granted. So guess what? Your days are over. And here
is the reason why. I was over—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Although you might have
announced your retirement, I th ink it is inappropriate fo r the member on his feet—
[Interruption] Which of us is standing, me or him? It is inappropriate for him to suggest
that your days are over.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Can I just say to the member
that that is a frivolous interjection. That is absolutely not necessary.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: The only reason why that member stood up is that it is getting
under his skin. It is getting under his skin. But guess what? Your skin is a white skin;
this is a brown skin.
Here is what you have got to know. I was at Caritas. There we were. Grant Robertson
was there. Guess what they said? Labour is happy to show th e statistics for M āori and
Pacific. It is happy to say that it want s to do everything for you. But guess what? The
new generation of M āori and Pacific say th at they have had enough of you saying that
you’re doing it for them.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: I apologise. We have had enough of the Labour Party saying
that it is doing it for us. It is time that we want to do it for ourselves, and that is the
reason why you will no longer have favour. That is the reason why you are going to lose
Māori and Pasifika votes coming to your table. This is the—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: I apologise. I am getting a little bi t excited here, but here is my
final point, which I want to put through. I just want to finally summarise with this.
The problem with the Labour Party is th is: I was born to a mother who was a
cleaner—who had been a cleaner all her life —and a father who was a labourer, and he
was in unions. I am the reality of their aspiration and their dream. But guess what? Now
that I have become the success of my family, you do not know how to talk to us. You do
not know how to talk to us. You don’t know how to work with us.
13258 General Debate 4 Sep 2013

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: The Labour Party does not know how to talk to us. The Labour
Party does not know how to work with us, a nd that is the reason why you will no longer
have the favour—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: —of Māori and Pasifika who will support you. Thank you.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Can I just say to the member
that I know that he was robust and passi onate about his speech, but every time the
member mentions the word “you”, you actuall y bring the Speaker in to the debate. You
can refer to a member on the other side or to the member’s party, but you must not bring
the Speaker into the debate.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. It is very good of you to give that ruling. Why di d you rule that my point of
order, which made exactly that point, was frivolous earlier? The member, because you
let him get away with it, did it 18 more times.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member is a very
experienced member.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
GAMBLING (GAMBLING HARM REDUCTION) AMENDMENT BILL
Third Reading

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Assistant
Speaker. Malo e lelei. I move, That the Gambling (Gambling Harm Reduction)
Amendment Bill be now read a third time . I stand today to speak to the third reading of
the Gambling (Gambling Harm Reduction) Amendment Bill. This bill has some history
that has got us to this point, so let me outline very quickly how we got here.
It is exactly 3 years ago that this bill was introduced. By the time of the general
election in 2011, however, there was still no sign  of the first reading in sight. It was for
that reason that the M āori Party specifically negotiated in its relationship accord
agreement with National that the bill w ould enjoy the support of the Government
through at least to the select committee. Five  months into the new term of Government,
the first reading occurred.
I said at the time that the bill marks a step towards advancing our kaupapa of
empowering communities to have a greater say about what happens in this area. Today
that statement remains true for me. This bill was always motivated by our campaign
against social hazards. I wa nt to acknowledge two women in particular who have
influenced my thinking in this regard. Th e first is the late Maureen Te Rere i Waho
Waaka, of T ūwharetoa and Te Arawa descent, w ho passed away just 3 months ago.
Maureen was a champion of the problem gambling kaupapa and was instrumental in
speaking out about access to casinos, gaming machines, and liquor outlets. The second
wahine toa is Dr Lorna Dya ll, who has led our thinking in reframing gambling from
being considered a normal recreational activity to one that is a social hazard. Just as
noxious weeds or pests create havoc in our na tural environment, gambling creates harm
within families, wh ānau, and communities, and can cause significant health and social
problems.
For the record, here is the state of th e nation: between 10,000 and 60,000 adults, or
0.3 percent to 1.8 percent, have a gambling problem in Aotearoa. The New Zealand
Health Survey showed that 3 percent of adults—that is about 130,000 people—have
experienced problems in the previous 12 months due to someone gambling, and 10,000
New Zealanders have engaged in illegal ac tivities because of their gambling. Every day
4 Sep 2013 Gambling (Gambling Harm Reduction) Amendment Bill 13259
$5.2 million is lost to gambling—$5.2 million every day. This is far more serious than a
chance win in a lottery.
Interestingly, the whole way in which we talk about gambling activities is so often
falsely painted as a story of prosperity. “Lady Luck is smiling on you.”, some would
say, or “It is your lucky day.” If things are going well, we are tempted to buy a Lotto
ticket to capitalise on our good fortune, but in doing so we willingly place emphasis on
the whim of the wheel of fortune to determine our future, rather than taking control and
shaping our future based on hard work and perseverance.
And yet the reality of problem gambling harm in our families is significant. The
Child Poverty Action Group summed this up by saying: “Sadly, it is usually the most
vulnerable children who pay the price of the recent proliferation of these hazards in low-
income communities. If children are to be pr otected from their effects, the government
must make greater efforts to support fam ilies and communities, and reduce access to
legal and illegal social hazards, including gambling, tobacco, alcohol, and high-priced
debt.”
So let me come back to the purpose of my bill, and what I think we have achieved. I
want to be clear that the bill was never about being anti-gambling—its focus was on
gambling harm. In that respect, I am consci ous that pokie machines are six times more
likely to be in poor areas th an in wealthy areas, and with in that about  a third of
moderate-risk gamblers are M āori. In effect, we are talk ing about a system in which
there is a wealth transfer from poor comm unities to well-off communities. It was for
that reason that I sought to phase out the corporate so cieties that distribute pokie
earnings, and ensure that 80 percent of ga mbling proceeds return to the communities
where the money was lost. My basic premis e was that the system incentivises the
exploitation of gambling addiction.
During the passage of this bill, submissions  and public releases alike revealed that
the system is rife with corruption and the misuse of public money. The Department of
Internal Affairs confirmed that in its 2012 review of venue cost schedules, which
revealed that approximately 750 venue subm issions could not yet be approved because
societies had not provided explanations or evidence in support of claims that costs
appeared high.
How does this revised bill address these issues? I truly believe that the bill takes
steps towards minimising the harm done to communities by gambling. The provisions
around local distribution and harm minimisation technology are still in the bill, only the
mechanism is a little bit different. I am ab solutely determined to keep pushing for the
use of the regulation-making power to introduce harm minimisation devices. A
regulation-making power is easier to use, easier to update, and enables a consistent
policy to be introduced nationwide.
The bill will also enable gambling venue s to transfer out of low socio-economic
areas and into areas where communities want th em to move. Councils, as a result of my
bill, will now have more tools to enable the transfer of gaming venues into other areas,
and I am confident that this will enable councils to further reduce the number of gaming
venues. More than anything else, however, my focus is on eliminating and ridding our
communities of gambling-related harm, and so my approach in this bill was on the basis
that other more wide-ranging reform would be announced. One of my ancestors Thomas

items.speaker: A Edison once said
items.text: “Our greatest weakness li es in giving up. The most certain way to
succeed is always to try just one more time. ” That has been the approach with this
particular bill.
The bill has been an enormous journe y. It has attracted a massive 29,438 form
submissions and 4,944 unique submissions  and supplementary information. The
Commerce Committee heard 159 submi ssions. The bill, it is fair  to say, has generated a
13260 Gambling (Gambling Harm Reduction) Amendment Bill 4 Sep 2013
fair bit of furious debate at hui, in the c ouncil chambers, in homes, and, indeed, in this
House. Does it do what I set out to do from the very beginning? Well, we were utterly
unsuccessful in our bid to remove the special status of the racing industry as a recipient
for the purpose of racing stakes, but was the c onversation an important one to initiate? I
believe so. Did we achieve the magic 80 pe rcent return? No. But the Government does
support the idea of a minimum percentage of proceeds being returned to the area where
they were raised, and that is an important philosophical discussion to have it inspire.
There is plenty more work to do. We are pl eased that this member’s bill, the first
Māori Party member’s bill to be passed into law, has generated a comprehensive
package of law reform. This includes incr easing the percentage of funding that goes
back to the community, introducing harm minimisation devices through regulation, and
giving councils more tools to shift venues out  of low socio-economic areas. It has been
a long struggle to achieve wh at we have, but we have neve r taken the focus off the best
interests of the people. We have appreciated the cooperation of the Minister of Internal
Affairs, the Hon Chris Tremain, and the efforts of the members of the Commerce
Committee, who all gave up so much time an d commitment toward s giving this bill
their full consideration. I thank them all. Ka nui te mihi.
But most of all I want to thank those w ho wrote in, those who appeared before the
select committee, those who went on talkback  radio, those who initiated the “People
Before Pokies” campaign, and those who cared. Can I also thank Graeme Ramsey of the
Problem Gambling Foundation for his advice. We might not have got to the place where
he wanted, but their work must be acknowledged. I also thank M āori Party staff—in
particular, Haimona Gardiner—for the work that they all did to give support to me.
We will not give up on the vital mission that we  have before us to continue to do all
that we can to prevent problem gambling harm from infesting our families and our
whānau and destroying our communities. I commend this bill to the House.

items.text: The question is that the
motion be agreed to. I call the—hang on, I ha ve just got to make sure we go according

items.text: You’re going to have two in s upport of it straight off. That’s
