items.text: Dean.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: Jacqui Dean. She brought this bill, the Conservation (Natural
Heritage Protection) Bill, to the House,  but it seems like only yesterday we were
debating the Waitaki Reserves—

items.speaker: Nicky Wagner
items.text: Four.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: The member Nicky Wagner is te lling me that Jacqui Dean has
had four members’ bills. Well,  frankly, I feel like taking a point of order about that,
because there are serious equity issues here. Someone is getting far too many members’
bills, and it is not me.
We are supporting this bill for obvious reas ons. It is a good bill, and all kudos to
Jacqui Dean, I think, for coming up with an  idea for a member’s bill that is very
practical, very beneficial, and makes a lot of sense. As members before me have
commented, this bill makes consistent a nd beefs up the penalty regimes for a whole
range of Acts that deal with  protecting our flora and fauna. The first thing I thought of,
actually, when I heard about Jacqui Dean’s bill was not the Czech botanists who stole
native orchids and so on, and not the German gecko-smuggler whom a number of
people have commented on. It made me think of a really sad inci dent that happened,
actually, in my electorate of Te Atat ū, where a couple of guys found a juvenile fur seal
that got caught up in their fishing net in Henderson Creek, a place quite close to where I
live and where I go kayaking quite often. Un fortunately, these guys clubbed to death
this baby seal with the oar of their dinghy a nd beat this poor baby seal senseless. This
was a couple of summers ago now. The 1-year -old fur seal was cared for at Auckland
Zoo, but it had a fractured cranium and a number of injuries, and it died within a couple
of weeks.
Those kinds of things happen from time to  time in New Zealand. They are awful
events. It is good that Jacqui Dean’s bill produces a set of penalties that will allow
enforcement to be carried out much more eas ily by the authorities,  and penalties that
will act as a proper deterrent. Having said all of these positive things about Jacqui
Dean’s bill, I do not want to be churlish and spoil the mood of the occasion, but I do
find there is an irony in the fact that th is bill cracks down on illegal whitebaiting and
fishing in marine reserves while the Gove rnment continues to allow gross overfishing
under the quota system of a number of our ma rine species. There is an irony in that
felling protected trees will be subject to in creased penalties in this bill, but this
Government has just demolished tree protec tion rules that would allow councils to
properly protect the urban forest.
The bill brings the Marine Mammals Protection Act under the new integrated penalty
regime, but this Government refuses to take  the most sensible a nd obvious measures to
protect the endangered M āui’s dolphin. It allows encroach ment into national parks, but
this Government spent a couple of years trying to convince New Zealand that we should
allow mining in national parks. So although Jacqui Dean’s bill is to be commended,
these ironies should be pointed out and s hould be considered by the general populace.
Thank you.
13298 Conservation (Natural Herita ge Protection) Bill 4 Sep 2013

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call the honourable
member Eugenie Sage. Tēnā koe.

items.speaker: Catherine Delahunty
items.text: No, no you don’t.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Catherine Delahunty—
Catherine Delahunty, absolutely. I am sorry, Catherine.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: That is fine. We have  had Eugenie; now it
is Catherine Delahunty’s turn. Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker. Tēnā koutou e te Whare
e p ōti i t ēnei p ō. We are also happy to be supporting Jacqui Dean’s bill, the
Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection) Bill. We really be lieve that we need to deal
with this issue by increasing penalties, which this bill does. I understand the passion of a
member like Jacqui Dean for a member’s bill. It is very hard to get one selected from
the ballot, and then when one does it is ve ry hard to get it thr ough the Parliament, so
this is very satisfying for her. I also have  had a bill before the Local Government and
Environment Committee, or it was before it, with less success. But I understand exactly
the passion that people feel about bills that  they have tried to shepherd through this
process.
This is an important bill because it sends  a good message to the courts. I think we
have heard a lot of detail. We do not need to  hear any more about it, actually. There has
been a lot of repeti tion tonight about some of the cl auses. I think it is all very
interesting. Clearly, the Local Government  and Environment Committee has done a
good job. The bill will be useful within its frame of reference and will send an important
message.
The whole issue of collecting illegally, as well as the strange brutality that people
sometimes demonstrate towards wildlife, are very old problems. In the 18 th century
European collectors started coming over to Ao tearoa and taking species, alive or dead,
and taking them back to Europe for their ow n purposes, for financial gain, and often for
museums. And so we have collectors su ch as Andreas Reischek who in the 19 th and
early 20th century robbed graves, took taonga kato a, and took various species with him
in the hope of making a name in Europe. In those days it was acceptable to a degree,
and the sad thing is that there is still a mark et for such a noxious trade. As others have
said, it is a big market, and it is still a major problem.
Our wildlife, although we are at the end of  the world, is extraordinarily unique, and
we need to defend it, and not ju st because of the description in the initial Department of
Conservation report on this bill. Conservation is defined in one of the office’s reports as
“a valued part of brand New Zealand”. That may be true but it is a very limited way of
looking at the world. One of the reasons that we are defending the wildlife is not just
that they are a brand but that they have intrinsic value in our community. They also
have intrinsic value to kaitiaki katoa, whose whakapapa goes back more than a thousand
years and has relationships with many of thes e taonga. So I think it is really important
that we get beyond the shallow and recognis e how deep the relationship is in this
country with some of these species—how unique, how important, and how vital it is
that not only do we not let people smuggle them but also we defend their right to exist.
The biggest threat to the species is not actually something this bill addresses, because
the biggest threat to the species is pest contro l and loss of habitat. That is why it is so
important that we commit to a coherent—not just a random but a coherent—approach to
conservation in this country, and that we recognise the article 2 rights of tangata whenua
in relation to taonga such as previously  mentioned by my Labour colleague, species
such as Māui’s dolphin.
If we look at these wildlife I think there are a lot of contradictions in discussing this
tonight, because, as much as the bill does  good work and we support it, it is very
interesting when we come to perhaps one of the most endangered species in this
4 Sep 2013 Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection) Bill 13299
country, the Archey’s frog, the pekahua, whic h is in my electorate—my area where I
live, not my electorate, but where I live. Th e Archey’s frog is the rarest frog on the
planet, yet this Government has given a pe rmit and supported a pe rmit for the mining
industry to go into that area and mine inside the Archey’s  frog’s habitat. On the one
hand we are doing the right thing, and on th e other hand we are actually allowing the
greater threat.
If we are going to allow the greater threat, we need to be  honest about that and say:
“Yes, it is OK. We are going to stop smuggli ng, we are going to stop acts of random
cruelty, but actually we are fine with destroying habitat.” I have a picture here tonight of
a postcard that I have got of the great spotted kiwi, an iconic species, which is going to
be damaged if we allow the mining of the Denniston Plateau. The green gecko, a
species that is intrinsic to the Denniston Plateau, and other species such as the great
spotted kiwi and the giant land snail are al l vulnerable not only because of bad people
and smugglers but also because we are actually committing other forms of vandalism
towards the conservation estate.
It is important that we acknowledge thos e contradictions a nd those threats to
biodiversity and remember that we are al l guardians and have a responsibility for
protecting these species for future generations. That is not a rhetorical statement. That is
about consistency and acting properly in terms of the environment, because these
species cannot flourish in isolation. They are not just iconic, charismatic species; they
are our environment. We need to protect th em. We commend the bill but we would like
to see a consistent approach to conservation from this Government before it is too late.
Kia ora tātou katoa.

items.speaker: Dr JIAN YANG
items.text: Ni hao. I rise to support the Conservation (Natural
Heritage Protection) Bill, in the name of the honourable member Jacqui Dean. This bill
sets out to better protect our special places  and species by increasing penalties for non-
compliance with the laws administered by the Department of Conservation. It also
implements a consistent approach to penalties across the amended laws.
As a first-generation immigrant from China, I always feel proud when I am talking to
visitors from China and, for that matter, to visitors from other pa rts of the world about
the environment of New Zealand. I can say for sure that other Chinese immigrants share
my feelings. You may be aware that there is currently a photo exhibition in Parliament.
The exhibition is called The Land of th e Long White Cloud—New  Zealand Through
Chinese Lenses. The exhibition consists of over 40 photographs, mainly of New
Zealand’s beautiful scenery, taken by Chinese photographers in New Zealand. I am very
proud that I initiated the exhibition. I was al so very grateful that  the Prime Minister,
John Key, and over 40 Ministers and MPs from  various parties came to the opening
ceremony of the exhibition. These photographers  speak loudly through their photos that
they love New Zealand, the land of the l ong, white cloud. I am very pleased that
Tourism New Zealand is interested in some of these photos and may use them to
promote New Zealand tourism. On behalf  of the photographe rs and the Chinese
community, I would like to thank my colleague Jacqui Dean for introducing this bill.
It is imperative that we look after our natu ral environment. It is  our greates t asset.
This bill proposes bigger fines and longer jail sentences for people who endanger our
wildlife or endanger our protected natural habitats. Some penalties currently in place are
far too low, and there are other inconsistencie s that need to be a ddressed. Our flora and
fauna are an important part of New Zealand’ s culture and heritage. We need to protect
our native species for future generations.
The Local Government and Environmen t Committee considered the bill and
recommended that it be passed with so me amendments. The committee took into
account a number of factors, in cluding intentionality and the type of offence. Offences
13300 Conservation (Natural Herita ge Protection) Bill 4 Sep 2013
motivated by commercial gain or reward will incur higher penalties. For instance,
bodies corporate could be fi ned up to $300,000 for commercially motivated offences.
The purpose of this is to create a stronge r deterrent and penalise the most serious
offending sufficiently severely.
As previous speakers have stated, this bi ll sends a strong message that we take the
protection of New Zealand’s wildlife and na tural areas very seriously. Actions that
damage or endanger our wildlife and natu ral areas put our protected species, good
international reputation, and tourism indus try at risk. This bill complements the
National-led Government’s efforts to boost th e conservation asset, better protect our
great outdoors, and strengthen conservation across New Zealand. We need a consistent
approach to penalties across the laws admini stered by the Department of Conservation.
This will ensure appropriate and effective penalties, punishments, and enforcement.
Vote Conservation is now $444 million, almost double the $226 million in 2001-02. We
are investing in recovery programmes for 35 percent more threatened species under
National. We also intend to review New Zealand’s threatened species management
framework. We are continuing to improve the environment and build a cleaner, greener,
and brighter future for all New Zealanders. I commend the bill to the House. Thank you.
Bill read a second time.
ELECTRICITY (RENEWABLE PREFERENCE) AMENDMENT BILL
First Reading
Debate resumed from 10 July.

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI
items.text: Sat sri akaal, Mr Assistant Speaker,
and thanks for the opportunity to participat e in the first reading of the Electricity
(Renewable Preference) Amendment Bill. Th e bill is in the name of Moana Mackey,
and National will be opposing this bill. This bill is one that is taking us in the reverse
direction. The bill is giving the wrong indica tion to the business co mmunity that if you
have the intention to expand your business, then the Government is not prepared to
guarantee you power supply. When I migrated to New Zealand I was very happy to see
that there were no power cuts, but some years later after arriving I started hearing that it
was possible we might have power cuts. I was very disappointed. Those days are not far
away if we adopt this bill, which bans our  thermal generation of electricity and will
ensure that we will have power cuts in this country.
The bill creates a preference of renewable electricity generation, which we agree to,
but we do not agree to the 10- year restriction on new base load fossil-fuelled thermal
generation. The ban would put th e security of power supply at risk. The ban on thermal
generation was initially  enacted as part of the Labour Government’s emissions trading
scheme in 2008 and subsequently repealed by the National Government in late 2008.
The National Government, as part of its gr owth agenda, has ensured the security of
energy supply, encouraged competition, and boosted the level of renewable energy. We
believe that it is the responsib ility of the Government to pr ovide infrastructure to the
businesses so that they can grow their bus iness and eventually help to grow the
economy. Under National the proportion of en ergy generated from renewable resources
has increased and is constantly above 70 percent—far higher than under Labour. We
have remained on track to achieve the goal of 90 percent renewable generation by 2025.
Labour had 9 years to make m eaningful reforms to energy and to increase renewable
energy. Instead, it made an arbitrary and hasty ban at the end of its term.
Gas and coal plants generate between 20 percent and 30 percent of our electricity.
Without this, the lights would not stay on. Thermal generation has been even more
4 Sep 2013 Electricity (Renewable Preference) Amendment Bill 13301
important during the times of peak demand. During the several winters between 2000
and 2008, gas and coal plants were at time s supplying 50 percent of New Zealand’s
electricity needs because of low hydro lake levels. To suggest that New Zealand could
do without thermal generation does not stand up to the facts. The ban on thermal energy
was totally unnecessary and threatened the security of supply. It is vital that we keep the
lights on, and I oppose this bill.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call the honourable
member Andrew Williams—nice haircut.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: Thank you very much, Mr Assistant Speaker.
It is a bit like your own one. I take a call on behalf of New Zealand First, and in this
instance we have determined that we will support the Electricity (Renewable
Preference) Amendment Bill through its first reading and hope that it does go to a select
committee. We do so on the basis that we f eel that on such an important subject New
Zealanders should be given the opportunity to have input and to have a good, national
debate about this particular subject.
Although we acknowledge the noble intent of  this bill, we do still have serious
reservations about its practicability. This bill would reinstate a 10-year ban on new coal
or gas-fired baseload power generation. Such  a ban existed briefl y under the previous
Labour Government. It has since been repe aled by this House. New Zealand First
reluctantly supported the original ban as pa rt of an agreement we reached with the
Labour Government in 2008 in respect of the emissions trading scheme. With the
benefit of hindsight, New Z ealand First acknowledges the problems that that ban
created. First of all, it put in jeopardy the s ecurity of supply. On average, one-third of
our nation’s electricity generation comes from thermal power. During the winter months
thermal generation can be as high as 50 percent. If it were not for pre-existing baseload
gas and coal-fired thermal pow er stations, such as those at Huntly and New Plymouth,
we could be at crisis point.
Second of all, it had an adverse effect on oil and gas exploration. Unlike the Greens,
New Zealand First is not anti-oil and is not anti-gas. We acknowledge the role that they
have to play in a modern economy. Of course , there must be restrictions on where and
how drilling can take place, and it must be  done in a sustainable, environmentally
friendly way. These regulations need to be strengthened, not weakened. The last thing
we want is our own Gulf of Mexico situati on. However, that being said, the oil and gas
sector provides enormous opportunities for employment and regional development in all
parts of New Zealand, potentially. In Tara naki alone the industry contributes $1.8
billion in GDP and 10,000 jobs. Possible new ventures in Northland and on the East
Coast could provide similar rewards. The rein stitution of this ban could put in jeopardy
any future discovery and development projects.
Finally, we do have some concerns that this bill, if it was to go through, could
actually increase dependence on the use of back-up coal generation by banning new-
generation gas capacity. Gas, although not 100 pe rcent clean, is a lot cleaner than coal.
Surely, it is better to use gas than to have no power at all, which is the dilemma we face
when considering this bill. New Zealand Fi rst would rather choose the lesser of two
evils than go back to the Stone Age, which is  where this bill could take us if the overall
situation is not addressed. In this respect, New Zealand First also has a policy whereby
in a future Government we would be seek ing to merge all the current State-owned
enterprise power generators, such as Meridian Energy and Genesis, and move them into
one single entity so that the security of s upply and the security of future provision of
energy sources would be under the one banner and controlled from one source, rather
than it being fragmented as it is today.
13302 Electricity (Renewable Prefer ence) Amendment Bill 4 Sep 2013
We want to encourage, however, the greater use of cleaner, greener, more sustainable
energy. New Zealand First certainly does support all endeavours to secure other
alternative additional means of providing en ergy to New Zealand industry and homes.
However, let us allow democracy to take its course. We feel that this is a good argument
and that the bill is worthy of  being considered by the public of New Zealand. We are in
favour of it going to a select committee so that the people of New Zealand can have
their say on this important subject. It is th e right of every New Zealander to have access
to reliable power, gas, and energy, and in th at respect we support th is going to a select
committee for consideration.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: A little bonus time on my feet tonight,
this time to speak against a very short- sighted—in my view—bill, the Electricity
(Renewable Preference) Amendment Bill, wh ich re-enacts the ban on thermal energy
generation. I fully understand that it re-enacts the ban for 10 years. But I think there are
a few other things that need to be pointed out  in the course of this discussion, and I just
want to pick up on one of the points that Andrew Williams, the previous speaker, made.
I see no reason for this bill to be forwarde d to a select committee. It just takes up a
whole lot more of this House’s time to deci de something where, frankly, we will end up
with the status quo, because common sense tells you that it needs to.
This type of bill, this type of acti on, along with the promotion of an advanced
emissions trading scheme system, puts a si gnificant amount of pressure on the average
New Zealand energy consumer. I am certainly not in favour of that. I am also not in
favour of either the previous speaker’s si ngle generator or th e proposal for a single
buyer for electricity.
I want to explain briefly why. In rural New Zealand our biggest power charges by far
are our lines charges. They have nothing to do with the electricity supply. If you want to
go and live in a place like  Taumarunui, National Park, Ōhākune, or any of those little
parts of New Zealand that are most important  to our tourism industry and to the future
of this country, you will find that your lines charges are significantly higher than your
electricity proportion of your bill. In fact, they do not get the lines charges in the
electricity portion of the bill; they get them  separately. So I guess that part of New
Zealand clearly understands where the cost of electricity is. It  is in the distribution cost,
for those of us in rural New Zealand. That is the challenge for the electricity industry, in
my view.
To ban thermal industry at a time when th ere is potential for modern, efficient,
environmentally friendly methods of therma l generation becoming available to us—and
it is quite possible that they will—I think would be irresponsible. It is a resource that, in
my view, we should use if we can use it sa fely and sustainably as a country. Again, the
previous speaker referred to some of the reasons for that. Clearly, some of us have
longer memories than others and can clearly  remember the time when electricity was
not something you took for granted at your gate, because some days it did not turn up.
In fact, in rural New Zealand we still find that on the odd occasion, but not because of a
shortage of power supply.
My region is covered in windmills, and alt hough I do not object to them, I can only
see them. I do not have to live beside them or  put up with the noise and the vibration of
them. I also think that in the future we are going to see windmills dotting New
Zealand’s landscape like derelict dairy factories in Taranaki. There will be one on every
corner and they will be rust ing. That is another reason that  I am not particularly in
favour of fiddling with the electricity generating process.
Not so long ago, in fact about  half an hour ago, we were talking about a bill that is
preserving our native and natural environment. I do not think that it is efficient for us to
use more of our—and I know they  are called sustainable res ources and things that will
4 Sep 2013 Electricity (Renewable Preference) Amendment Bill 13303
last for ever, but in fact a lot of them do not, and I referred to the windmills earlier. I
think we have a responsi bility to future generations to look at alternat ives and to use
those resources that we have in abundan ce in New Zealand, provided we use them
responsibly and use them in a manner that provides for a sustainable future for this
country. I do not think it is our business to run Parliament  as a type of a game of
monopoly. I think bills like this tend to do that, to some extent.
This bill achieves little, as there will be  no new thermal genera tion or electricity
plants built in New Zealand in the next few years—probably for 10 years—because we
have sufficient electricity in this country to sustain our future. I would not like to be the
person trying to obtain a consent to build one of those plants under the current
environment anyway. I cannot support this bill and that is me.

items.speaker: Hon MARYAN STREET
items.text: It gives me great pleasur e to rise to speak to
the Electricity (Renewable Preference) Am endment Bill, sponsored by my colleague
Moana Mackey. Much in all as I admire the member who has just resumed his seat, Ian
McKelvie, I have not heard such an anti quated speech in a long time. We should be
preparing for the future. [ Interruption] We should be prepari ng for the future. We
should be looking ahead.
The Government currently has two targets. Th e first is that 90 percent of electricity
generation will be from renewable sources  by 2025. That was a Labour Government
target. It was set when Labour was in Gove rnment, and it is very pleased that the
National Government has seen fit to retain that target. The second thing the Government
has got as a target is to reduce greenhous e gas emissions by 50 percent by 2050. But it
has no plan to achieve either of these targets.  What we have are two targets out there in
the future with no stepped plan to achiev e them. We agree with  90 percent generation
from renewable sources. Goodness knows we  have got wind, marine, geothermal,
hydro, and, hopefully, more solar power coming on stream in the future.
The opposition to this bill is based on antiquated views of how this country might
sustain its energy supply in the future. I w ould like to draw what the bill does to the
attention particularly of the member Ka nwaljit Singh Bakshi, who seemed to have
ignored the fact that the bill quite explicitly says that this  does not include “an existing
plant” or “an electricity genera tion plant that is operating in  accordance with a contract
for reserve energy entered into by, or on behalf  of, the Commission”. So let us not hear
any more of this nonsense about the lights goi ng out. Let us not hear any more of this
nonsense. It does not affect existing plants.
What the bill does do, in fact, is put b ack in place the Electricity (Renewable
Preference) Amendment Act, which the Labour  Government enacted over 5 years ago.
That established a restriction on new baseload fossil-fuelled thermal electricity
generation. Can I be any clearer than that? It established a restriction for 10 years on the
building of new baseload fossil-fuelled ther mal electricity generation plants. It was a
start to try to wean ourselves off our fossil fuel dependence and begin to apply the kind
of pressure that we need if we are ev er going to reduce our greenhouse gas emissions
and if we are ever going to transition to a society that is not dependent on fossil fuels.
I am just astonished that members opposite cannot bring themselves to support this
bill. They will have to, at some stage, be  dragged, kicking and screaming, into the 21 st
century, or into the next decade, anyway, of the 21 st century. The future is not in
electricity generation using fossil fuels. The future is in renewable energy. Fortunately,
New Zealand has an abundance of  all those things that other countries cry out for in
order to complement or overt ake their use of fossil fuels for electricity generation and
allow them to move their countries and th eir economies on beyond using fossil fuels for
electricity generation.
13304 Electricity (Renewable Prefer ence) Amendment Bill 4 Sep 2013
This is a ban for 10 years. It is something that expires at the e nd of that 10 years,
because at that point we will be able to assess the extent to which we have been able to
move towards sustainable renewable electricity generation. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr JIAN YANG
items.text: I rise to oppose the Electric ity (Renewable Preference)
Amendment Bill. This member’s  bill in the name of Labo ur MP Moana Mackey will
create a preference for renewable electricity  generation by a 10-year restriction on new
baseload fossil-fuelled thermal electricity  generation. The ban on thermal generation
was initially enacted as part of the Labour Government’s emissions trading scheme in
2008 and subsequently repealed by the Nationa l Government in late  2008. This bill re-
enacts that ban.
A ban on thermal generation is unnecessary. A ban would also put security of supply
at risk. New Zealanders need to be assured that during the harsh wi nters that can grip
many regions we have a backup when hydro la kes and wind generation are low. During
several winters between 2000 and 2008 gas and coal plants were at times supplying
over 50 percent of New Zealand’s electricity needs because of low hydro lake levels.
The bill defines “fossil fuel” in new section 62C, inserted by clause 5, as natural gas,
coal, petroleum, any refined petroleum products, or any ot her obligation fuel. Gas and
coal plants in New Zealand generate between 20 percent and 30 percent of our
electricity, and they play a crucial role in keeping New Zealanders warm in winter and
our lights on for households and businesses to function.
The portion of energy generated from rene wable sources has risen under a National
Government. It is consistently above 70 per cent, which is far highe r than it was under
Labour. Just last month the Environment Cour t gave the go-ahead to Genesis Energy’s
Castle Hill Wind Farm project, which is  north of Masterton and east of Eket āhuna, to
build 286 turbines, which will power around 370,000 homes. National remains
committed to renewable energy, and we remain on track to reach the aspirational goal of
90 percent renewable generation by 2025.
Our reforms have controlled runaway incr eases in power prices. In fact, price
increases have halved, yet we have still maintained investment in generation and
transmission. New Zealanders are savvy a nd are increasingly taking advantage of
greater competition and switching compan ies for a better deal, as shown by the
popularity of the What’s My Number website . The Government has already undertaken
major electricity reforms to increase comp etition and improve security of supply.
Labour and the Greens have already done thei r best to scaremonger and deter investors
with their plans to nationalise the energy sector. Their power plan will kill competition
and raise prices. This bill, which seeks to  ban thermal generation, would cause further
economic mayhem. I will not be supporting the bill. Thank you.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: On behalf of my colleague Moana
Mackey, I now have the opportu nity to speak fo r 5 minutes in reply to the other
contributions that have been made in th is debate on the Electricity (Renewable
Preference) Amendment Bill.
What has become abundantly clear, lis tening to the members opposite speaking on
the debate, is that none  of them have actually read th e bill. They have been clearly
reliant on notes put together by someone in th eir research unit who also has not actually
read the bill. As they talk about security  of supply, and particularly talk about the
importance of having access to thermal generation in the case of a dry year when supply
might be at risk, they seem to have missed the fact that that is specifically allowed for in
the bill. There is a provision in there th at allows for non-renewable energy during a
power crisis. So it is already covered. It a llows for the running of plants that combine
non-renewable and renewable sources. It allo ws for one thermal generating plant to
replace another thermal generating plant where that is needed for upgrades and so on.
4 Sep 2013 Electricity (Renewable Preference) Amendment Bill 13305
There are plenty of provisions in this bill that allow for security of supply. What the
bill seeks to achieve is to ensure that future demand is met through renewable
electricity. There is no good reason, in a c ountry like New Zealand, why we should not
be doing something like that. When we alr eady get such a high percentage of our
electricity from renewable energy anyway, we  should be aspiring to do even better. We
should be aspiring to have a fully renewable electricity sector over time. Of course no
one is saying we are going to switch off the thermal generation plants, which is what
some of the members over there have suggested—clearly, another example that they did
not actually read the bill. There is no suggestion from anybody that that is what is going
to happen. What we are saying is  that as we try to meet future demand in the electricity
system, we should do that from renewable sources, and that is something that I think is
a perfectly legitimate thing to ask for.
This is the second time that we have debated this bill in this House, because the first
time it was in my name and it was in the la st term of Parliament. Gerry Brownlee came
in and he spoke against it, and he said “We don’t need this bill because, although the
Government does support the idea of meeting future demand through renewable
electricity”—they do actually  agree with that; you would not know that from listening
to some of their speakers earlier tonight. But Gerry Brownlee, a couple of years ago,
was saying that the Government did believe in meeting future demand through
renewable electricity, and he said that the way it was going to achieve that was by
putting a price on carbon. Well, how has th at worked out? The price on carbon has
collapsed. It is now providing no real incentive for renewable electricity.
Actually, now the Government has gone ev en further and said that it does not
actually believe in renewable electricity at al l. It is talking about how it supports this
kind of 90 percent aspirational ta rget, but it is just not go ing to do anything to ensure
that we get there. But, actually, we need to  get there. As a country, New Zealand should
be leading by example when it comes to renewable electricity. We have no good reason
not to, and we know that in th e long-term interests of New Zealand, that is something
that we should be doing. In the long term, re newable electricity is actually going to be
significantly cheaper. In fact, much of our re newable electricity is already significantly
cheaper than thermal generation, and that is one of the reasons why we have this very
distorted market, which the Labour Party is committed to addressing through the NZ
Power policy. At the moment, New Zealande rs are paying a higher price for their
electricity than they need to because the current market is failing. Yet the Government
over there, once again, is not willing to do anything about that.

items.speaker: The Labour Party has made it very clear
items.text: we support renewable electricity. We are
willing to do something about that. We suppor t New Zealanders paying a fair price for
their electricity. They are certainly paying well above a fair price at the moment, and we
are willing to do something about that. In the meantime , the National Government’s
response is “Just leave it to the market. The market will sort everything out.” So if
future demand for electricity is met thr ough further use of non-renewable resources,
which costs more money to consumers in th e long term, the National Government says
that is perfectly OK. We on this side of the House say, no, that is not OK. We want
renewable electricity. We want  cheaper electricity. We wa nt New Zealanders to be
paying lower prices in their power bills each  month. That is something that we are
willing to do something about, while the cu rrent Government si ts on its hands and
simply says “It’s OK, the market will sort it all out.” The market is not sorting it all out.
The market is failing in electricity, and th e Government needs to intervene to do
something about that.
The NZ Power policy will result in New Zealand consumers paying $200 to $300 per
year less than what they are paying now. That is something we are very proud of. It also
13306 Electricity (Renewable Prefer ence) Amendment Bill 4 Sep 2013
has the potential to create 5,000 more jobs. Th at is not something you hear the National
Government talking about much these days. It  does not seem to believe in creating new
jobs any more. John Key is probably the onl y person in world history who hosted a job
summit that resulted in higher unemployment,  but that has certainly been the track
record of this National Government.
We on this side of the House say we shoul d get active. We should ensure that New
Zealand’s electricity future is a renewable el ectricity future. We should ensure that we
bring down the price of power for New Zeal and consumers. We on this side of the
House are willing to do something about that.
A party vote was called for on the question, That the Electricity (Renewable
Preference) Amendment Bill be now read a first time.
Ayes 59
New Zealand Labour 34; Green Part y 14; New Zealand First 7; M āori Party 2;
Mana 1; Independent: Horan.
Noes 61
New Zealand National 59; ACT New Zealand 1; United Future 1.
Motion not agreed to.

SUMMARY OFFENCES (POSSESSION OF HAND-HELD LASERS)
First Reading

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call on members’ order of
the day No. 4. Just before doing so, I want  to advise the House that the honourable
member Cam Calder will be using a visual aid, and to advise the member that it must be

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: I move, That the Summary Offe nces (Possession of
Hand-held Lasers) Amendment Bill be now read a first time.  I nominate the Transport
and Industrial Relations Committee to consider the bill.
I am privileged to have my office in the vibrant and diverse electorate of Manurewa.
The Manurewa electorate is overflown by upwards of 140,000 flights annually. Some
years ago I became aware of the risks posed to pilots, on their final approach, from
cockpit illumination with r eadily available handheld lase r pointers. Laser pointers,
though used by teachers, researchers, astronomers, and university lecturers in the course
of their daily work safely and without incident , assume an altogether more sinister role
when used to illuminate a plane’s cockpit. The sequelae, temporary vision loss in its
various forms, can have poten tially catastrophic consequences not only for those in the
aircraft but also for those in the commun ities around airports or on the approach paths
thereto. I was surprised to learn that each y ear in excess of 100 cases of handheld lasers
being used in such a manner have been documented in New Zealand alone, and the
incidence of their misuse shows no sign of decreasing.
I consulted with the New Zealand Air Line  Pilots’ Association, the Civil Aviation
Authority, and the Police Association. All agreed  that preventative measures need to be
put in place to reduce the chance of laser mi suse occurring. I discussed my concerns
with Ministers. After a period of consultation, on 15 May 2013 the Government
4 Sep 2013 Summary Offences (Ha nd-held Lasers) Amdt Bill 13307
announced that handheld lasers strong enough to be a hazard to aircra ft will be subject
to new import, sale, and supply controls unde r health and customs legislation. Their use
will be restricted to authorised users who have a legitimate purpose, such as
astronomers, researchers, and the New Z ealand Defence Force. An order under the
Customs and Excise Act 1996 and regulati ons under the Health Act 1956 to control
these devices are being drafted, and I expect that the new controls will be in effect by
the end of the year. These new regulations  mesh with and complement the proposed
Summary Offences (Possession of Hand-held Lasers) Amendment Bill.
The regulations will dramatically reduce the number of new lasers coming into the
country and people who will have access to them. There are, however, an unknown
number of handheld lasers already in Ne w Zealand. The legislation will make it
perfectly clear that it is unacceptable to be in possession of these handheld lasers in a
public place without reasonable excuse. The bill is designed to have a preventative
aspect, and will reduce the likelihood of mi suse by individuals of any of the unknown
thousands of laser devices already in our country. My research indicated that the
problem with laser pointer misuse had been acknowledged all over New Zealand and,
indeed, was a well-known problem internationally.
I was concerned to find there was currently no legislation to control the carriage of
such a potentially offensive weapon, despite section 13A of the Summary Offences Act
being in force for the carriage of a knife in  a public place. Society has decreed, in its
wisdom, that it is not in the interests of th e safety and well-being of our citizenry if
knives are routinely carried on one’s person. Obviously, knives can all too readily inflict
grievous wounds or potentially be used to kill an individual; hence, carrying them
routinely is discou raged by section 13A. Section 13A  could be said to have a
preventative role. The legisla tion is not designed to captur e a family going on a picnic
that needs a sharp knife to cut a tomat o, and is applied with due cognisance of
circumstances.
Obviously, a high-powered laser pointer has the potential to  cause visual damage to
an individual, but because the range of a la ser pointer can be measured in miles, the
potential collateral damage of such visual dist urbance to the pilot of an aircraft or to the
driver of a large vehicle is huge. A simple  trawl on the internet shows that high-
powered lasers of up to 800 milliwatts in power are readily available. They are
advertised as 532-nanometre green lasers to impress even the serious professionals. The
light can burst balloons, melt plastic, light matches, and have a range of up to 60
miles—yes, 60 miles. Handheld lasers range in  size from a small pen to a torch, and are
readily carried in a pocket. Yet because of their ability to interfere with a person’s
vision at a huge distance, they are potentially far more dangerous than a simple knife. It
is ridiculous that something so small can  pack so much punch and yet its carriage
remains completely uncontrolled.
Laser pointers are available in a wide range  of strengths, from a power level of less
than 0.39 milliwatts, as seen in compact disc  players or laser printers—so-called class
1—right up to class 4, with a level of 500 milliwatts or above, which may cause eye and
skin damage, even from reflected beams. Outdoor and industrial laser pointers belong to
this category. But as we have mentioned, many lasers of this  strength are easily carried
in the hand and are virtually indistinguishable from the lower-powered variety.
Already this year we have seen furthe r instances of where laser misuse has
endangered the safety of the public in New Zealand. Members of the House may recall
that in late April two aircraft were target ed at Wellington Airport,  one on take-off, the
other on landing. Airline company Jetstar la belled the laser st rike as highly
irresponsible. Commenting on the laser strike from the airport, Police Sergeant Brett
Cousins stated that it could have caused multiple fatalities. Stu Julian from the Airline
13308 Summary Offences (Hand-held  Lasers) Amdt Bill 4 Sep 2013
Pilots’ Association observed that it had not yet associated lasers with the same
capability as a gun, but that they can cause loss of life.
In early March the New Zealand Herald outlined an instance from the “Surely Some
Mistake” file. Two particularly challenged young men thought it fun to engage with the
police’s Eagle helicopter. Not content with illuminating the cockpit once, they did it
half a dozen times, for 5 to 10 seconds at a time, and continued, according to the Crown
prosecutor, to inflict very  intense flashes on the cockpit even as the chopper was
hovering above them directing a ground patr ol on to them. In his summing up and
sentencing, Judge Nevin Dawson said: “The results could have been catastrophic. There
was potential for very tragic consequences. People need to get the message that this
offending is not just a foolish prank.” Speaking of the case, New Zealand Airline Pilots’
Association President, Glen Kenny, said: “T he handheld laser thre at is an on-going
public safety concern and today’s result shoul d strengthen the safety message and make
people think twice before they shine a laser at an aircraft”. Because these individuals
were apprehended actually using a laser agains t a moving vehicle or aircraft, they were
successfully prosecuted under section 270 of the Crimes Act.
It is pertinent to note that  cheap, common, and r eadily available class 3 lasers with a
power less than 5 milliwatts can have a range  in excess of 11,000 feet, or 2 miles. This
can seriously interfere with a pilot’s night vi sion. I have here in my hand one of these
lasers of that nature. You can see how strong th at light is if I just shine it directly above
us, and that can go for some 11,000 feet.
What is the effect of a laser beam when illuminating an aircraft cockpit on a night
approach to an airfield? Temporary vision loss is, of course, one of the most common
and potentially dangerous effects of cockpit illumination. It can be associated with
glare, flash blindness, blind spots, or after-images. Glare is considered to be a temporary
disruption in vision, caused by th e presence of a bright light within an individual’s field
of vision and lasting as long as  the light exposure. In flas h blindness the temporary loss
of vision persists after the source of illumination has been removed. Blind spots are
similar to flash blindness, but only part of the visual field is affected. An after-image is
an image that remains in the visual field after exposure to a bright light. The US Federal
Aviation Administration simulator studies a bout the effects of laser illumination during
final approach show that a legal laser of th e size I just demonstrated can easily cause
glare and distract pilots up to 3,700 feet and remain a di straction hazard up to 11,000
feet—in excess of 2 miles. Near flash blindne ss is a potential problem in the last stages
of final approach at a range of 350 feet. T hus, we have a wide ra nge of effects from
laser misuse determined by the distance away an affected person is from the source of
the laser beam.
As I have mentioned, serious consequences  can also eventuate if laser beams are
shone into the eyes of the driver of any m oving vehicle. Imagine the consequences if a
beam were shone into the eyes of the driver of a fuel tanker on a motorway at night.
Imagine the consequences and the potential for tragedy of that event.
The purpose of this amendment bill is to have a preventative aspect and to reduce the
likelihood of a person being in a position to carry out an offence with any one of the
countless thousands of devices already in New Zealand. The bill will complement the
effect of regulations restric ting the importation, sale, and acce ssibility of laser pointers.
The bill will send a clear message that these devices are not toys, that they have the
potential to cause significant harm, and that, without reasonable excuse, their carriage in
a public place will not be tolerated. I seek the support of the House for the Summary
Offences (Possession of Hand-held Lasers) Amendment Bill to progress to the select
committee.
4 Sep 2013 Summary Offences (Ha nd-held Lasers) Amdt Bill 13309

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise
and speak to the Summary Offences (Possession of Hand-held Lasers) Amendment Bill,
in the name of Dr Cam Calder. I want to put  on the record, to start with, that Labour
will support this bill going to the Transpor t and Industrial Relations Committee. There
are several reservations that we have with this legislation that we think would need to be
tidied up at the select committee, but we do congratulate the member on pursuing a
worthy subject. There have been, as I thi nk the member probably pointed out in his
speech, over 100 incidents of lase r strikes against aircraft in  the last year. There have
been a handful of convictions related to that, and I think it  is important to acknowledge
that this bill does not make it an offence to perform one of these laser strikes against an
aircraft; that is already an offence. Recently, a young man was sentenced to 4½ months’
home detention, having been ca ught and convicted of carrying out a laser strike against
a landing aircraft.
What this bill seeks to do—and, as I said, it is a worthy cause—is to reduce the
likelihood that people will be able to have la sers and use them in an inappropriate way,
such as a laser strike against an aircraft or, indeed, as the member raised, a strike against
a land motor vehicle such as a truck. I thi nk the member used the example of a fuel
tanker. That would probably be the most di sastrous possible outc ome. But, indeed, I
know that a number of airline pilots have sa id that really it is  only a matter of time
before somebody tries this against a moving vehicle, and the consequences of that
could, indeed, be quite disastrous.
What this bill does is make it an offen ce liable to imprisonment for a term not
exceeding 3 months or a fine not exceed ing $2,000 for anybody who, in a public place,
without reasonable excu se—which is an interesting phras e that I am sure is open to
interpretation—has any handheld laser in his or her possession. We think that this bill is
probably a bit too broad. This is going a little bit too far into the realms of a nanny State
for the National members to support a bill that  would ban the possessio n of all lasers in
a public place without some reasonable excuse.
In fact, it actually goes much  further than the Government itself has indicated that it
is comfortable with, with the regulations that it recently brought in, as announced by the
Associate Minister of Health Jo Goodhew,  that can be made under the health and
customs legislation to regulate the impor tation and possession of lasers. What the
Government did and what the Minister announ ced was exactly what the airline pilots
have been calling for, which is tighter regu lations on the most powerful lasers. In fact,
the controls that the Government has in troduced will be applied to handheld laser
pointers with a power output greater than 1 milliwatt—I assume it is probably not a
megawatt—in line with the approach taken in Australia and with recommendations
from the World Health Organization. The new restrictions will not cover lower-powered
laser pointers used as presentation aids, or t hose used with survey equipment or at rifle
sites. That to me seems to be the sensible balance that needs to be achieved. Without a
change that better reflects the Government’s  approach to those regulations in this
legislation, Labour would find it difficult to su pport this bill past the select committee
process, but I believe that the member would be open to some debate and conversation
around how we can better target this legislatio n at the lasers that actually cause harm
and not inflict unnecessary regulation on pe ople who have these lower-powered lasers
for perfectly legitimate reasons.
There are very few occasions to have the higher-powered lasers in a public place. I
know that some astronomers use them, and certainly astronomy teachers use them to
actually point out constellati ons in the sky for young child ren who are learning about
the night sky, and I am sure there would be other reasons related to  survey equipment,
etc., where it would be reasonable to ha ve the higher-powered lasers. Many people
13310 Summary Offences (Hand-held  Lasers) Amdt Bill 4 Sep 2013
would carry around a little pen laser pointer that is not capable of creating the havoc that
the member in charge of this bill is con cerned about. As is alwa ys the case with this
kind of regulation, it is about getting the bala nce right. We want to reduce the harm, we
want to reduce the likelihood that people will be able to carry out these laser strikes, but
we do not want to unnecessarily burden people who have the lower-powered lasers for
perfectly legitimate reasons.
It is a bit of a surprise that a Nationa l member would support such a Draconian
approach, but we will get that sorted out at the select committee. I can see some of the
National gentlemen who are on the committ ee and who are looking forward to fixing
that bill up, I am quite sure.
It is a bit unfortunate, I think, that the Government has been so slow to respond to
this issue. It was not until May this year that Jo Goodhew announced the regulations
that will come into effect. They have not yet come into effect, and it is anticipated that
those regulations will come into effect to wards the end of this year. The Government
has left it to a member’s bill and it has left it to a backbencher, with all due respect to
Cam Calder, to promote this legislation. It has left it at the mercy of the ballot and left it
at the mercy of the members’ orders, and we  know that it takes an awfully long time for
a member’s bill to rise to the top of the Order Paper and get its first reading debate.
I would have thought that this Government wo uld take the safety of airline pilots, of
passengers on aircraft, and, indeed, of road users much more seriously and would have
promoted this type of legislation much s ooner than it has. There has been a dramatic
increase in the incidence of these laser strikes from only a handful in 2006 to over 100
in the last year. The evidence was clear that this was a growing problem. The airline
pilots came and spoke to us in the O pposition, and I know that they spoke to
Government members. They did not do a big kind of public ra h-rah campaign. They
came and spoke to us very reasonably and as ked the Government to promote legislation
that would increase their safety, and yet the Government sat on its hands. It sat on its
hands until May this year be fore announcing regulations—regulations that have not yet
come into force—and the supporting legislation that Cam Calder is promoting has come
to the House only because a backbench MP decide d to put this bill in the ballot. He was
lucky enough to have it come out—very luc ky to have it come out —and it has finally
made it to the House tonight, in  September. I think that th at tells you a little something
about this National Government’s approach to safety, particularly transport safety.
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 10 p.m.

Sweden—Dr Anders W Jonsson, Riksdag 
Mr SPEAKER: Honourable members, I have much pleasure in informing the House 
that a parliamentarian from the Riksdag of Sweden, Dr Anders W Jonsson MP, is 
present in the gallery. I am sure that members would wish that he be welcomed. 
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Skycity, Convention Centre—Advice to Cabinet 
1. METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Minister for Economic 
Development: When he said, in relation to the Skycity convention centre deal, “the 
negotiated significant additional harm-minimisation measures that apply to all gambling 
machines in that casino will together act to reduce harm” was he basing his claim on the 
Health Ministry’s gambling harm minimisation team’s advice; if not, why not? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for Economic Development) : My comment was 
based on information contained in the regu latory impact statem ent prepared by the 
Ministry of Business, Innovation and Empl oyment following consultation with, and 
summarising advice received from, the followi ng agencies: the Ministry of Justice, the 
Gambling Commission, the Ministry of Pacific Island Affairs, Te Puni Kōkiri, Treasury, 
the Ministry of Social Devel opment, the Ministry of Women’s Affairs, the Office of 
Ethnic Affairs, the Department of Internal  Affairs, the New Zealand Police, and the 
Ministry of Health. 
Metiria Turei: Why did the Minister exclude from the regulatory impact statement 
the advice from the Ministry of Health that it was “doubtful” voluntary pre-commit 
cards would reduce harm, and that Skycity wa s already using the t echnology so it was 
not, in fact, either new or additional? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : I think the member misunde rstands the role of the 
regulatory impact statement. The regulatory imp act statement is prepared by officials, 
and it is a summary of all the different o fficial advice that comes from different 
agencies. 
Metiria Turei : Why, then, did the Minister sign off on the regulatory impact 
statement, which excluded the advice from the Ministry of Health  that doubling of host 
responsibility staff at the Skycity Casino was likely to have at best a minimal effect? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : Again I think the member is misunderstanding the role of 
the regulatory impact statement, which is to collect together the information supplied by 
different departments. It may come as a surpri se to the member that I have not read the 
advice from every single one of those agencies. The regulatory impact statement— 
Hon Trevor Mallard: Why not? You’re in charge. 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : Do not be a clown, Trevor. The regulatory impact 
statement is put together as a summary of the different agencies. 
Hon Trevor Mallard : Is it not his practice to read the advice from all officials on 
bills? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: It is not my practice to read advice to individual Ministers 
from every single agency for a paper that I am taking to Cabinet. I very much doubt that 
13230 Questions for Oral Answer 4 Sep 2013 
it is any Minister’s practice, and it was certa inly not the practice of previous Ministers 
in the previous Government. 
Metiria Turei: When the Minister told this House that Cabinet had considered “all 
of the risks and benefits of the social a nd economic impacts” of this deal, was he 
mistaken, or was he deliberately misleading the House? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : Well, neither. Cabinet, as always in these situations, 
receives a Cabinet paper, and in appropria te cases, including this one, a regulatory 
impact assessment, which different agencies contribute to and which is summarised by 
the lead agency, is then taken to Cabinet. That is what occurred in this case, as occurs in 
a whole range of other cases. It has to be said that the regulatory impact statements have 
been a heck of a lot better prepared unde r this Government than under previous 
Governments. 
Metiria Turei : What other advice did the Minister choose to leave out of the 
regulatory impact statement, and did part of it include  the advice on the intended 
reduction in the Television New Zealand (TVNZ) dividend as a result of the sale of land 
to Skycity under the convention centre deal? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : Again, for the member’s benefit, if she had listened to a 
previous answer, she would notice that the suppo sition contained in the first part of that 
supplementary question is incorrect. In rela tion to the second part of the supplementary 
question, she is also incorrect because, in ac tual fact, in terms of the forgiveness of 
dividends, which was flagged, potentially, some time ago, that is for the opportunity for 
TVNZ to renovate its building next door, whic h I think is a fantastic outcome. It has 
sold some land to Skycity as part of the convention centre arrangements and it is getting 
an opportunity to make a much-needed renovation to its facilities. 
Metiria Turei : Were Cabinet and his caucus colleagues made aware of the likely 
significant extra cost of this need to induce TVNZ by way of a reduced dividend 
expectation to move out of part of its cen tral Auckland premises to make way for the 
convention centre deal before they voted for the bill? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : I completely reject the asse rtion that the member makes. 
The reality, as I have made quite clear, is that the convention centre could proceed with 
this extra piece of land or without, and it is quite obvious that it could do so. TVNZ was 
given the opportunity to sell the land. It we nt to its shareholding Ministers and said: 
“Well, look, we would like to renovate our building. Would you support us in doing 
so?”. As has been said publicly for some time now, it was indicated that shareholding 
Ministers would support that, and so out of this we will get a fantastic convention centre 
for New Zealand based in the middle of Auckland City, generating jobs, generating 
tourism opportunities, and also TVNZ, next door, will get an upgrade of its building, 
including earthquake strengthening and future -proofing. So it is all working out as a 
pretty big win-win. 
Metiria Turei: Did the Minister advise the Minister of Broadcasting, Craig Foss, last 
year about the possibility of a reduced divi dend from TVNZ due to the Skycity deal, 
given that Mr Foss demanded at least 9 percent in dividends from TVNZ in December? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : I think the matter was raised by TVNZ with its 
shareholding Ministers a reas onably short time ago. There wa s a letter that went back, 
which I referred to publicly, I think, from memory, a coupl e of months ago, and it was

Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM (Green) : It may not realise it, but this Government has 
ruled out New Zealand’s support for any military  action in Syria that is not authorised 
by the United Nations Security Council. Let me read out to the House the Government’s 
answer to my question on action over Syri a of 15 February 2012: “7. Dr Kennedy 
Graham (Green) to the Minister of Foreign Af fairs: Will he give an assurance that New 
Zealand’s armed forces will not be used in any possible military intervention in Syria in 
violation of the United Nations Charter? Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman (Minister of 
Defence) on behalf of the Minister of Fore ign Affairs: Yes. Dr Kennedy Graham: Is he 
then, … in a position to confirm that the G overnment does not support external military 
involvement in Syria unless it responds to a United National Security Council resolution 
authorising it—that is to say, no coalition of the willi ng is legal without that mandate? 
Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman: New Zealand alwa ys follows the United Nations Security 
Council resolutions, so we would not be doing anything in violation of that.”  
I congratulate the Government . Let me point out why it was so insightful 18 months 
ago. Syria is a global human tragedy in a de fining moment in the modern struggle for 
global peace and justice. There can be no la wful military action in Syria without proof 
to the United National Security Council of  chemical weapon use and by whom. And 
even if proof is provided, there can be no military action without authorisation by the 
council. That is not a matter of political judgment; it is a non-negotiable legal 
requirement. The US is advancing the argument that there is a legal justification based 
on humanitarian intervention. Th at is incorrect. That doct rine, more appropriately 
known today as responsibility to protect, does not trump the United Nations Charter. 
That was made clear in United Nations Ge neral Assembly Resolution 60/1, paragraphs 
138 and 139, in 2005. The US is being somewh at disingenuous here. Even if the UN 
were to authorise military action, thereby ma king it legal, it would require a separate 
decision on the part of each country as to  the political merit of becoming directly 
involved. The doctrine lays down six criteria fo r such a judgment. The critical issue is 
whether the action proposed would relieve sufferi ng rather than cause more. It is almost 
certain it would not.  
If we ever needed a lesson in caution, it was the illegal military action against Iraq by 
the US, the UK, and Australia in 2003. The evidence adduced to the council as proof of 
a nuclear weapon programme proved to be fa lse—indeed, part-fabrication. For its part, 
the much maligned United Nations Security Council declined to agree to such an 
invasion. That was not simply a French veto. A majority of the council opposed military 
action, yet those three countries proceeded without UN authorisati on, and illegally. If, 
in the case of Syria, the council chooses not  to act because of a veto, it does not mean 
the council is dysfunctional a nd not doing its job. It means the council has decided not 
13254 General Debate 4 Sep 2013 
to act. The council would actually be doing its job, just as it did with Iraq in 2003. Many 
in the West might resent that fact, retaining a 20 th century sense of mo ral and political

UN, and they refuse to this day to change the charter when the prospect of doing so is 
before them. They refuse to surrender or ev en circumscribe their veto, and then, when 
they confront a situation, wh en another permanent member casts a veto, they seek to 
circumvent that veto by acting around it. S o, if the US and the UK are concerned about

surrender the veto, or, at least, by agreeing to  its strict circumscription to only when 
their vital interests of survival are at stake.  Let this Parliament have a chance to debate 
this matter when it next meets.

GAMBLING (GAMBLING HARM REDUCTION) AMENDMENT BILL 
Third Reading 
TE URUROA FLAVELL (Co-Leader—M āori Party) : T ēnā koe, Mr Assistant 
Speaker. Malo e lelei. I move, That the Gambling (Gambling Harm Reduction) 
Amendment Bill be now read a third time . I stand today to speak to the third reading of 
the Gambling (Gambling Harm Reduction) Amendment Bill. This bill has some history 
that has got us to this point, so let me outline very quickly how we got here.  
It is exactly 3 years ago that this bill was introduced. By the time of the general 
election in 2011, however, there was still no sign  of the first reading in sight. It was for 
that reason that the M āori Party specifically negotiated in its relationship accord 
agreement with National that the bill w ould enjoy the support of the Government 
through at least to the select committee. Five  months into the new term of Government, 
the first reading occurred.  
I said at the time that the bill marks a step towards advancing our kaupapa of 
empowering communities to have a greater say about what happens in this area. Today 
that statement remains true for me. This bill was always motivated by our campaign 
against social hazards. I wa nt to acknowledge two women in particular who have 
influenced my thinking in this regard. Th e first is the late Maureen Te Rere i Waho 
Waaka, of T ūwharetoa and Te Arawa descent, w ho passed away just 3 months ago. 
Maureen was a champion of the problem gambling kaupapa and was instrumental in 
speaking out about access to casinos, gaming machines, and liquor outlets. The second 
wahine toa is Dr Lorna Dya ll, who has led our thinking in reframing gambling from 
being considered a normal recreational activity to one that is a social hazard. Just as 
noxious weeds or pests create havoc in our na tural environment, gambling creates harm 
within families, wh ānau, and communities, and can cause significant health and social 
problems.  
For the record, here is the state of th e nation: between 10,000 and 60,000 adults, or 
0.3 percent to 1.8 percent, have a gambling problem in Aotearoa. The New Zealand 
Health Survey showed that 3 percent of adults—that is about 130,000 people—have 
experienced problems in the previous 12 months due to someone gambling, and 10,000 
New Zealanders have engaged in illegal ac tivities because of their gambling. Every day 
4 Sep 2013 Gambling (Gambling Harm Reduction) Amendment Bill 13259 
$5.2 million is lost to gambling—$5.2 million every day. This is far more serious than a 
chance win in a lottery.  
Interestingly, the whole way in which we talk about gambling activities is so often 
falsely painted as a story of prosperity. “Lady Luck is smiling on you.”, some would 
say, or “It is your lucky day.” If things are going well, we are tempted to buy a Lotto 
ticket to capitalise on our good fortune, but in doing so we willingly place emphasis on 
the whim of the wheel of fortune to determine our future, rather than taking control and 
shaping our future based on hard work and perseverance.  
And yet the reality of problem gambling harm in our families is significant. The 
Child Poverty Action Group summed this up by saying: “Sadly, it is usually the most 
vulnerable children who pay the price of the recent proliferation of these hazards in low-
income communities. If children are to be pr otected from their effects, the government 
must make greater efforts to support fam ilies and communities, and reduce access to 
legal and illegal social hazards, including gambling, tobacco, alcohol, and high-priced 
debt.”  
So let me come back to the purpose of my bill, and what I think we have achieved. I 
want to be clear that the bill was never about being anti-gambling—its focus was on 
gambling harm. In that respect, I am consci ous that pokie machines are six times more 
likely to be in poor areas th an in wealthy areas, and with in that about  a third of 
moderate-risk gamblers are M āori. In effect, we are talk ing about a system in which 
there is a wealth transfer from poor comm unities to well-off communities. It was for 
that reason that I sought to phase out the corporate so cieties that distribute pokie 
earnings, and ensure that 80 percent of ga mbling proceeds return to the communities 
where the money was lost. My basic premis e was that the system incentivises the 
exploitation of gambling addiction.  
During the passage of this bill, submissions  and public releases alike revealed that 
the system is rife with corruption and the misuse of public money. The Department of 
Internal Affairs confirmed that in its 2012 review of venue cost schedules, which 
revealed that approximately 750 venue subm issions could not yet be approved because 
societies had not provided explanations or evidence in support of claims that costs 
appeared high.  
How does this revised bill address these issues? I truly believe that the bill takes 
steps towards minimising the harm done to communities by gambling. The provisions 
around local distribution and harm minimisation technology are still in the bill, only the 
mechanism is a little bit different. I am ab solutely determined to keep pushing for the 
use of the regulation-making power to introduce harm minimisation devices. A 
regulation-making power is easier to use, easier to update, and enables a consistent 
policy to be introduced nationwide.  
The bill will also enable gambling venue s to transfer out of low socio-economic 
areas and into areas where communities want th em to move. Councils, as a result of my 
bill, will now have more tools to enable the transfer of gaming venues into other areas, 
and I am confident that this will enable councils to further reduce the number of gaming 
venues. More than anything else, however, my focus is on eliminating and ridding our 
communities of gambling-related harm, and so my approach in this bill was on the basis 
that other more wide-ranging reform would be announced. One of my ancestors Thomas 
A Edison once said: “Our greatest weakness li es in giving up. The most certain way to 
succeed is always to try just one more time. ” That has been the approach with this 
particular bill.  
The bill has been an enormous journe y. It has attracted a massive 29,438 form 
submissions and 4,944 unique submissions  and supplementary information. The 
Commerce Committee heard 159 submi ssions. The bill, it is fair  to say, has generated a
